Applied Materials Commits $5 Billion to India as Chip Manufacturing Expands
Vardah Gill 
September 21, 2026 3 min read 
AMAT 
-8.16% 
Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMAT ) plans to invest $5 billion in India over the next decade, expanding its research, supply-chain, and workforce capabilities as India tries to establish itself as a major semiconductor manufacturing hub. 
The announcement came at SEMICON India, where more than 600 companies from 52 countries participated. India has committed more than $21 billion in semiconductor incentives and expects domestic semiconductor consumption to reach $110 billion by 2030. Applied's investment is therefore aimed at building a longer-term presence in an emerging semiconductor ecosystem rather than generating an immediate revenue contribution. 
Applied Materials (AMAT) - Among Billionaire Steven Cohen’s Top 11 Dividend Stock Picks India Investment Could Expand Applied Materials' Long-Term Growth 
The investment could give Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT) an early position in a market that is attempting to diversify semiconductor production beyond established hubs such as China and Taiwan. India has already approved 12 semiconductor projects under its incentive program, while commercial production has begun at some chip-packaging facilities. As more fabs and packaging facilities become operational, Applied could capture demand for deposition, etch, inspection, packaging, and other process equipment. Its existing portfolio spans these manufacturing stages, giving the company multiple opportunities to participate as India's ecosystem develops. 
The investment also fits Applied's current growth cycle. In fiscal Q3 2026, revenue reached a record $9.12 billion, up 25% year over year, while gross margin rose to 50.3% and operating income increased to $3.08 billion. Applied generated a record $3.04 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter. The company has said strong AI-driven demand is supporting leading-edge logic, DRAM and advanced packaging, while it expects semiconductor-equipment growth to remain strong through 2027. A larger Indian R&D and supply-chain footprint could therefore support capacity and customer diversification as semiconductor investment expands globally. 
Applied Materials Faces Execution Risks With Its India Expansion 
The biggest risk is that India's semiconductor ambitions may take considerably longer to translate into equipment revenue. Reuters reported that India still has no large-scale chip fabrication facility in commercial production, while Tata Electronics' planned $10 billion fab in Gujarat has been delayed by nearly two years. That means Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT) could commit substantial capital well before the local customer base generates meaningful equipment demand. The $5 billion commitment spread over ten years also represents a long-duration capital allocation rather than an immediate earnings catalyst. 
Story Continues 
The investment could also pressure returns if India's manufacturing buildout progresses more slowly than expected. Applied already faces significant geopolitical exposure: its SEC filing says export restrictions have limited its China market and increased exposure to Chinese competitors. The company also paid $253 million in 2026 to settle a U.S. Commerce Department inquiry involving certain China shipments. At the same time, investors have questioned whether Applied can maintain its recent growth and margins; Reuters noted that its fourth-quarter revenue forecast of $10.25 billion came with a roughly 50.4% margin outlook amid increasing competition. Expanding in India could diversify geopolitical exposure, but it does not eliminate execution, regulatory, or capital-allocation risks. 
Conclusion 
Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT)'s $5 billion India commitment strengthens its long-term positioning in a market targeting $110 billion of semiconductor consumption by 2030, while aligning with the company's need to expand capacity as AI drives demand for advanced chips and packaging. The main limitation is timing: India's fab ecosystem remains immature, with major projects still facing delays. Consequently, the investment is more directly relevant to Applied's long-term geographic diversification and competitive positioning than to near-term revenue or earnings.

Texas geothermal company gets $135 million funding boost to continue superhot rock exploration at Oregon’s Newberry Volcano
By Monica Samayoa ( OPB ) 
Sept. 22, 2026 1 p.m. Updated: Sept. 22, 2026 8:41 p.m.
A geothermal developer has secured more than $135 million to reach new depths and advance superhot rock development in Central Oregon’s Newberry Volcano .
Texas-based Mazama Energy says the investments, made by major venture capital companies and oil businesses, will allow it to continue its quest to drill thousands of feet below the surface to harvest heat to generate renewable power.
THANKS TO OUR SPONSOR:
Become a Sponsor 
FILE - Aerial shot of Mazama Energy’s pad 29 on September 9, 2025. The company, which is digging deep to harness heat from hot rocks, has announced recent investments of more than $100 million to support its work.
Brooke Herbert / OPB 
The funding will allow Mazama to create its Project Ceres — a horizontal well development which the company says has the potential to generate 15 megawatts of electricity in 2027. That would be enough to power the equivalent of 4,500 average households.
“We see this as an investment in Oregon’s energy future,” said Pete Lumley, Mazama’s communications director.
Deschutes County Chair Commissioner Phil Chang concurred, applauding the investment for both its local and its potential global impact. 
If geothermal companies eventually deliver as much electricity as they forecast, Chang said, the region could become a net-exporter of energy and, in turn, “our community can make a meaningful contribution to the efforts to fight climate change globally,” he said.
Drilling deeper into the earth to harvest heat for energy has recently been gaining steam in the U.S. as the next big renewable energy source.
Conventional geothermal energy has been used for decades, including in Klamath Falls, but it requires a natural reservoir of hot water or steam near the earth’s surface to generate electricity, which restricts where this technology can be used.
Now, many companies are working to figure out ways to access the heat beneath our feet to use as a baseload, or continuous, energy source, beyond what conventional geothermal can deliver.
Besides Mazama, there’s been a flurry of investment in geothermal opportunities in Oregon’s Newberry Volcano and across the Northwest. 
Quaise Energy, another Texas-based geothermal development company, has developed millimeter wave drilling technology to reach superhot rock depths. The company is currently working on developing a 50-megawatt geothermal plant called Project Obsidian by 2030. 
Virginia-based Hexagon Energy announced earlier this month that it plans to explore geothermal opportunities on Weyerhaeuser Co.-owned lands in Oregon and Washington. And in August, the U.S. Bureau of Land Management sold geothermal development rights to 9,500 acres on Mount Hood National Forest to unnamed developers for more than $1 million.
New technology to meet a growing need
The boost in funding in geothermal is coming as regional power planners, researchers and independent analyses show the Pacific Northwest is going to need a lot of energy to keep up with growing demand , including from new large power users like data centers .
Mazama Energy is attempting to build what it says will be the hottest engineered geothermal system ever through an enhanced geothermal system called superhot rocks .
“We’re not just drilling a hotter hole, we’re engineering the whole system,” Lumley told OPB on Friday. “It’s a sustainable energy source, and it allows us to extract the heat from the hot rock below and turn that into electrons.”
THANKS TO OUR SPONSOR:
Become a Sponsor 
FILE - A blue cylinder billows steam, indicating success for Mazama Energy’s pilot project on September 9, 2025. 
Monica Samayoa / OPB 
The company does this by drilling thousands of feet beneath the earth’s surface and injecting water into an engineered hot rock reservoir. The water absorbs the earth’s heat and returns to the surface as steam. That steam drives a turbine to generate power. The steam is then cooled, converted back into water, and reinjected into the reservoir to allow the cycle to continue.
“It’s continuous, unlike some other renewables, where they’re cyclic through the day — if the sun isn’t shining or the wind isn’t blowing, we don’t have the power,” Lumley said.
Last year, the company drilled more than 10,000 feet below the surface, reaching underground areas with temperatures as high as 629 degrees Fahrenheit. 
Then, the company drilled a second well to the same depth in about two weeks, or 80% faster than the first well, Lumley said.
The company is pushing to drill faster as it works to make the case for its business model and demonstrate that it has the potential to compete with oil and gas, he said.
Drilling costs are more than $100,000 per day, so moving faster also means substantial savings for the company, Lumley said.
Now, Mazama is going deeper.
In its next phase, called Project Athena, the company is going to drill more than 15,000 feet deep. 
Deeper means hotter rock, Lumley said, and that means more heat can be harvested for energy use.
“We need to drill fewer wells,” he said. “We need to use less land, and we use less water during the drilling and the production of the electrons.”
If successful, Lumley said Mazama Energy could hit two milestones — generating 50 megawatts by 2029 and up to 200 megawatts by 2030. That’s enough energy to power about 200,000 average households.
And if that is successful, Lumley said the company forecasts it could produce 10 gigawatts of continuous commercial energy at Newberry some day.
Boosting the local workforce and economy
The $135 million investment toward Mazama’s geothermal development is a reflection that this form of energy is now technologically and economically mature and viable, which can have many benefits for the local community, Deschutes County Chair Chang said Monday.
“Adding cost-effective renewable generation of this type is pretty exciting, not just for Central Oregon, but for the state,” he said. 
Chang said these kinds of investments in the region could play out big for the residents, meaning potential for a lot of high-skill and high-wage jobs. 
He’s also hopeful geothermal companies based in the region can reach what is known as a “ benefits agreement ” with local communities. That could include a commitment to invest in the development of a renewable energy workforce.
“This could be training programs in high schools, community colleges, and OSU Cascades,” Chang said. That could “produce a workforce not just for enhanced geothermal systems, but also for a variety of other kinds of energy generation and energy efficiency type projects.”
Editor’s note: This story was updated to add more details about the financial benefits Mazama Energy receives when it drills geothermal wells more quickly.

Arkema Adds 3,000 m³ GAA Storage Capacity in South Korea
Emilia Lanier 22-Sep-2026 
Arkema secures 3,000 m³ of glacial acrylic acid storage in Ulsan, strengthening Korean supply reliability and Northeast Asia logistics.
Arkema is strengthening its glacial acrylic acid (GAA) supply network in South Korea by securing 3,000 cubic meters of new tank storage capacity at the Ulsan HDOT terminal. Announced on September 21, 2026, the move is aimed at improving local supply reliability and supporting rising demand for acrylic-based applications across Asia. 
The newly secured storage tank will function as a local hub for Arkema’s GAA business in Korea, allowing the company to maintain material closer to domestic customers. The additional infrastructure is expected to provide greater flexibility in inventory management and logistics while enabling Arkema to offer more consistent and responsive deliveries to Korean buyers. 
The investment also forms part of Arkema’s broader strategy to strengthen its presence in Northeast Asia, where Korea, Japan and China remain important markets for acrylic monomers. By establishing additional local storage capacity, Arkema can improve the connection between its production facilities, regional logistics network and customer operations. 
Hervé Castres Saint Martin, Group President for Acrylic Monomers at Arkema, said the Korean project would strengthen synergies across Northeast Asia while bringing the company closer to customers. He added that the enhanced regional footprint would support customer-driven application development, collaborative innovation and greater supply resilience. 
Arkema’s acrylic monomer operations in Asia are supported by its production facility in Taixing, China, which serves customers across China, Japan, Korea and Southeast Asia. The company is using the expanded regional network to strengthen its ability to respond to changing customer requirements while developing opportunities in acrylic-based applications. 
The Korean storage project comes as demand for acrylic materials continues to expand across applications including coatings, adhesives, construction materials and other specialty products. While the new tank does not represent additional production capacity, localized inventory could help reduce logistical constraints and improve delivery responsiveness during periods of tight regional supply or transportation disruption. 
Arkema is simultaneously advancing sustainability across its acrylic value chain. The company has been implementing ISCC+ Mass Balance certification across its acrylic monomer production sites worldwide, supporting customers seeking lower-carbon and more circular material solutions. 
Arkema generated approximately €9.1 billion in sales in 2025 and operates in around 55 countries with approximately 20,700 employees. The company continues to focus on specialty materials, with its Adhesive Solutions, Advanced Materials and Coating Solutions businesses accounting for around 85% of group sales in 2025. 
Product and Chemical Price Impact 
Arkema’s additional 3,000 m³ GAA storage capacity in Korea should improve local inventory availability, delivery reliability and supply flexibility without directly increasing regional production. The facility may help Korean acrylic acid consumers reduce exposure to shipment delays and short-term logistical disruptions. For GAA and acrylic acid markets, the move is broadly supply-supportive and could moderate localized tightness when inventories are adequate. However, the impact on GAA and downstream acrylic monomer prices is likely to remain limited initially because the project adds storage rather than production capacity. If stronger Asian demand coincides with production outages or constrained imports, improved inventory positioning could nevertheless reduce the severity of short-term price spikes in Korea.

title: Rare Earth Metal and Alloy Capability Outside of China in September 2026 - InvestorNews
query: ("Hitachi Metals" OR "Proterial") ("press release" OR "investor relations" OR earnings OR announcement OR investment OR expansion OR acquisition OR partnership OR Korea) after:2026-09-01 before:2026-10-01
content_text:
Rare Earth Metal and Alloy Capability Outside of China in September 2026
Critical Minerals & Rare Earths , Market Opinion 
Jack Lifton
September 21, 2026 
1 Comment
“The rare earth supply chain outside China is much thinner than the headline numbers suggest. Announced capacity is not production, and neither a mine, an oxide refinery nor a magnet plant proves that rare earth metal is actually being made.” — Jack Lifton, Co-Chair, Critical Minerals Institute (CMI)
I asked myself: What is the current production capability and capacity for rare earth metals and alloys outside China? And exactly where are the production facilities?
As of September 2026 , the list is much shorter if “production facility” means a site that actually makes a rare earth metal or alloy , rather than one that only mines ore, separates oxides, or manufactures finished magnets. Below, operating means the metal/alloy step has been demonstrated or is in production; announced capacity is not actual output. Public disclosures are uneven, so this is a documented inventory, not a guaranteed census of every small or captive plant.
Japan
Facility Status Metal/alloy activity 
Santoku, Kobe-area operations (plants in Kobe, Akashi, Miki and Tsuruga) Operating A longstanding producer of rare earth metals, NdFeB magnet alloys, samarium cobalt alloys and hydrogen storage alloys. Santoku says it commercialized molten salt electrolysis for rare earth metals and mass production of strip cast magnet alloys. Its public material does not give a reliable plant-by-plant tonnage breakdown. Santoku became part of Proterial Magnetics in 2026. 
Shin-Etsu Chemical, Takefu, Fukui Prefecture Operating integrated materials/magnet site Shin-Etsu lists rare earth metals among its products and describes Takefu as handling raw material refining and magnet material production. The public sources I found do not isolate its current metal or alloy making capacity from finished magnet capacity. 
Shin-Etsu, additional Fukui plant Announced In June 2026, Shin-Etsu confirmed a new domestic rare earth refinery intended to secure supply for its rare earth products and magnets. Its precise metal/alloy process, capacity and opening date were not disclosed, so I would not yet count its tonnage as new metal capacity. 
Japan also has major magnet manufacturers such as TDK and Proterial. Making a magnet necessarily involves magnetic material, but I have not counted each magnet factory as a separate, publicly verified oxide-to-metal or merchant alloy facility.
South Korea
Facility Status Metal/alloy activity 
Korean Metals Plant (KMP), Ochang, Cheongju Operating; expanding Built by Australian Strategic Materials Ltd. (ASM) and now owned through ASM by Energy Fuels Inc. (NYSE American: UUUU | TSX: EFR), following its August 2026 acquisition . It makes NdPr metal and NdFeB strip-cast alloy ; it has also made initial commercial sales of dysprosium and terbium metals. Energy Fuels states 1,300 tonnes/year of existing NdFeB alloy capacity , with expansion to 3,600 tonnes/year targeted for commissioning as early as late 2026. ASM reported about 45 tonnes of NdFeB alloy and NdPr metal dispatched in Q2 2026 —a useful reminder that nameplate capacity is not output. 
A naming trap: KSMM/KSM Metals and the Ochang Korean Metals Plant refer to the ASM project’s Korean operating structure , not a second independent plant.
Rest of the world 
Country and facility Status Metal/alloy activity 
United Kingdom — Less Common Metals (LCM) , Cheshire Operating Converts oxides and recycled inputs into rare earth metals, master alloys and strip-cast products, including NdPr, Dy, Tb and Sm-related products. USA Rare Earth, Inc. (Nasdaq: USAR), its owner, reports roughly 2,500 tonnes/year of total rare earth and critical mineral metal/alloy capacity —not all necessarily magnet rare earths. It reported a first commercial yttrium metal pour in April 2026. 
United States — MP Materials “Independence,” Fort Worth, Texas Operating; ramping Integrated metal making, NdFeB alloy flake production and magnet manufacturing . Commercial metal production began in 2024; first alloy flake on commercial equipment followed in 2025. MP Materials Corp. (NYSE: MP) has also selected nearby Northlake, Texas , for its announced “10X” expansion; published magnet targets should not be mistaken for a separately disclosed metal tonnage figure. 
Thailand — Neo Magnequench, Korat Operating alloy powder producer Makes rapidly solidified NdFeB magnetic alloy powder for bonded magnets. This is alloy/powder production , not oxide-to-metal refining ; its dependence on supplied metal feedstock matters when judging supply chain independence. 
Germany — Remloy, Bitterfeld Developed recycling/alloy plant; commercial scale-up to verify Remelts end-of-life magnets into NdFeB alloy powders for bonded and hot-deformed magnets. Mkango Resources Ltd. (TSXV: MKA) cited 500 tonnes/year of plant capacity in its 2026 acquisition materials. This is a recycled alloy route, not primary oxide-to-metal conversion. 
Vietnam — Shin-Etsu Magnetic Materials, Hai Phong Operating integrated magnet site Shin-Etsu describes an integrated route from rare-earth refining/recycling through magnet production. Public disclosures establish the integrated site but do not cleanly quantify a stand-alone metal/alloy stage, so I would not add its magnet tonnage to metal/alloy totals. 
Canada — Saskatchewan Research Council, Saskatoon Near commissioning An integrated processing facility with a metal-smelting stage , intended to produce magnet-grade NdPr metal as well as Dy and Tb oxides . SRC says commissioning is planned for December 2026 and operation after ramp-up in 2027. The heavy rare earth oxides are not yet heavy rare earth metals . 
United States — REalloys, Euclid, Ohio Limited existing downstream activity; larger heavy-metal project announced REalloys Inc.  (NASDAQ: ALOY) describes current specialty heavy rare earth metal/alloy and component operations. Its proposed larger Dy/Tb oxide-to-metal facility , in partnership with SRC, is a distinct scale-up: equipment is to be built and initially tested in Saskatchewan, then moved to Ohio. I would not treat the announced large-scale capacity as operating. 
France — LCM Europe, Lacq Announced USA Rare Earth, Inc. (Nasdaq: USAR) plans a 3,750-tonnes/year metal-and-alloy plant alongside Carester’s separate oxide-processing project. The oxide plant’s planned commissioning does not mean the LCM metal plant is operating. 
United States — USA Rare Earth, Blacksburg, South Carolina Announced Planned integrated refined-metal, strip-cast alloy and magnet operation. The company targets 5,000 tonnes/year of strip-cast, metal and alloy and commissioning beginning in 2028 ; that figure groups products rather than specifying tonnes of rare earth metal alone. 
United States — Energy Fuels’ proposed American Metals Plant Planning Intended to replicate capabilities developed at Ochang. An ASM planning presentation described an initial 2,000 tonnes/year of alloy , expandable to 4,000, but site, funding, construction and ultimate capacity remain project decisions—not production. 
Vietnam — LS Eco Energy/Lynas project Announced A planned plant to convert Lynas-supplied rare earth oxides into metals for magnet supply chains. The partners had announced investment and cooperation by March 2026; I did not find a verified operating output figure. 
India — government-backed integrated magnet scheme Program announced, individual facilities not yet established India’s government explicitly identifies industrial-scale oxide-to-metal and metal-to-alloy capacity as a domestic gap . Its incentive program seeks 6,000 tonnes/year of integrated finished NdFeB magnet capacity across selected projects—not 6,000 tonnes of metal capacity. 
The central takeaway is that Japan’s established producers, Ochang, LCM in Britain, MP Materials in Texas, and Thailand’s alloy-powder operation are the clearest sizeable operating nodes in this inventory. Many of the larger numbers now circulating—France, South Carolina, the Ochang expansion and the proposed American plant—are future nameplate capacities . And neither an oxide refinery such as Estonia’s Silmet nor a finished magnet plant, on its own, proves that rare earth metal is being made at that site. The IEA likewise identifies metals and alloys as a particularly constrained link in the non-Chinese supply chain.

BASF Extends Partnership With Charlotte Motor Speedway STEAM Program
Monday, September 21, 2026
Students explore what happens when dry ice and water mix during the launch of the Mobile Pit Stop, a partnership between BASF and Charlotte Motor Speedway’s STEAM program. The event was held at BASF’s corporate office in Charlotte and provided students a variety of hands-on activities to learn about science, technology, engineering, arts and math. CMS photo 
BASF , a leading global chemistry company, and Charlotte Motor Speedway’s STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Art and Math) program announced today the extension of a partnership will continue STEAM’s mission to enhance and educate children K-12 about STEAM initiatives in and around motorsports. The partnership, which supported programs for more than 30,000 students last year, continues to open the doors to possibilities for children in the greater Charlotte area, surrounding communities and neighboring states.
The Charlotte Motor Speedway STEAM program is the only year-round STEAM program within motorsports in the country. In 2025, the program hosted 30,394 people across 280 daily programs, five special events and summer camps, and its largest STEAM Expo at Charlotte Motor Speedway to date, with 19 participating schools. Five additional schools took part in the inaugural North Wilkesboro Speedway STEAM Expo.
This year, the program has already hosted 257 daily programs with schools coming from across North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, Georgia, Florida and Virginia.
“The impact of Charlotte Motor Speedway’s STEAM program is measured not only in the thousands of students who walk through our doors, but in the curiosity, confidence and possibilities they take with them when they leave,” said Melissa Stirewalt, STEAM manager. “What began with just 579 children in 2011 has grown into the only year-round STEAM program in motorsports, reaching students from across the Southeast and beyond. Every year, we see more schools, more students and more opportunities to show young people that the skills they’re learning in the classroom can open doors to careers and possibilities they may have never imagined both inside and outside of motorsports.”
Through this extended partnership with BASF, Charlotte Motor Speedway’s STEAM program will receive $50,000 for its year-round programming. This partnership will continue the mission of providing hands-on learning to help students connect real-world applications during its year-round programming. Students engage through several interactive STEAM stations focusing on topics such as forces and motion, push and pull, physics and engineering as it relates to Motorsports.
The partnership will also help with the relaunch of the STEAM mobile program, Mobile Pit Stop, that allows CMS to have a further impact in our community. The mobile unit will focus primarily on the Charlotte-Mecklenburg school district and surrounding counties, targeting fourth through sixth grade students. Students will participate in hands-on experiments to discover the fascinating world of polymers, test how materials respond to different forces, and uncover the science behind race car tires. The program will conduct up to two site visits per week with a maximum of 60 students each visit.
“BASF is dedicated to enhancing the pathway to STEAM careers by emphasizing science education from an early age,” said Denise Hartmann, BASF Senior Vice President – Dispersions & Resins Division, Americas. “We are excited to deepen our engagement with the Charlotte community by introducing young minds to the world of chemistry through our expanded partnership with the Charlotte Motor Speedway. Our interactive Kids’ Lab experiments and educational programs through this collaboration aim to ignite a passion for scientific exploration and highlight the vast opportunities in STEAM-related fields.”
In addition to STEAM’s Mobile Pit Stop program and daily program at Charlotte Motor Speedway, students are able to attend the annual STEAM Expo, held during the Bank of America 400 race weekend, and other special events.
The STEAM Expo was first featured in 2018, with more than 1,200 students from Virginia and the Carolinas learning through interactive displays. It has continued to grow over the last eight years, welcoming as many as 4,000 children annually with a variety of educational booths highlighting a range of Speedway partners such as the local colleges and branches of the United States Armed Forces.

Bruker Receives Order for High-Field NMR Systems for Major Upgrade of Magnetic Resonance Research Infrastructure at UC Berkeley
Provided by Business Wire Sep 21, 2026, 11:00:00 AM 
Bruker Receives Order for High-Field NMR Systems for Major Upgrade of Magnetic Resonance Research Infrastructure at UC Berkeley 
New high-field NMR instrumentation strengthens biomolecular and materials science research at the UC Berkeley Pines Magnetic Resonance Center 
Bruker Corporation (Nasdaq: BRKR) today announced a multi-system order from the University of California, Berkeley for high-field Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) instrumentation at the Pines Magnetic Resonance Center. The investment will enhance access to next-generation NMR technologies, including 800 MHz–class instrumentation. These capabilities strengthen research in chemistry, materials science, structural biology, and related fields across UC Berkeley and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.
This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260921533654/en/ 
Bruker MAS CryoProbe for high-sensitivity solid-state NMR research
The Pines Magnetic Resonance Center (PMRC) comprises faculty, technical staff, and postdoctoral researchers. The PMRC Core NMR facility is a leading shared NMR resource, offering 24/7 access to researchers from academia, national laboratories, and industry. By integrating high-performance instrumentation with method development, training, and analytical services, the facility enables multidisciplinary studies of molecular structure, dynamics, and function.
The investment is centered on a Bruker AV NEO-X 800 MHz spectrometer equipped with a cryogenically cooled MAS CryoProbe, complemented by several additional NMR systems and upgrades supporting solid-state, solution-state and Dynamic Nuclear Polarization (DNP) research.
“This expansion will propel UC Berkeley, an institution with an exceptionally strong tradition in magnetic resonance, to the forefront of high-impact innovation for years to come,” said Professor Tatyana Polenova, Director of the Pines Magnetic Resonance Center. “By integrating next-generation NMR and DNP with advanced methodologies, including fast magic-angle spinning, MAS CryoProbes, computational analysis, and quantum sensing and control, we are opening new avenues to address previously inaccessible structural and mechanistic questions across a broad range of systems, including intact cells and organisms, macromolecular assemblies, bio-inspired materials, inorganic materials, and molecules at interfaces and surfaces.”
“Translating cutting-edge NMR technologies into robust, reproducible workflows is critical,” said Dr. Patrick Wikus, Head of Product Management at Bruker BioSpin. “The AV NEO-X platform provides a robust foundation for advanced solid-state, solution-state, and DNP NMR experiments, combining highest performance and enabling new capabilities with reliable day-to-day operation.”
The UC Berkeley NMR order exceeds $6 million and is expected to be delivered in 2027.
About Bruker Corporation – Leader of the Post-Genomic Era (Nasdaq: BRKR)
Bruker is enabling scientists and engineers to make breakthrough post-genomic discoveries and develop new applications that improve the quality of human life. Bruker’s high-performance scientific instruments and high-value analytical and diagnostic solutions enable scientists to explore life and materials at molecular, cellular, and microscopic levels. In close cooperation with our customers, Bruker is enabling innovation, improved productivity, and customer success in post-genomic life science molecular and cell biology research, in applied and biopharma applications, in microscopy, as well as in industrial and cleantech research, and semiconductor metrology in support of AI. Bruker offers differentiated, high-value life science and diagnostics systems and solutions in preclinical imaging, proteomics and multiomics, spatial and single-cell biology, structural and condensate biology, as well as in clinical microbiology and molecular diagnostics. ARKEMA STRENGTHENS GLACIAL ACRYLIC ACID SUPPLY IN KOREA WITH NEW STORAGE TANK
PR Newswire   Sep. 21, 2026 08:00
451
ULSAN, South Korea , Sept. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- On September 21, 2026, Arkema announces that it has secured new tank storage capacity of 3,000 m³ for Glacial Acrylic Acid (GAA) at the Ulsan HDOT terminal in Korea. The new facility will be part of Arkema's broader efforts to support growing demand for acrylic-based applications across Asia. 
Arkema Enhances GAA Supply with New Storage Capacity in Korea 
The new tank will serve as a local storage hub for Arkema's GAA business in Korea. With domestic storage capacity in place, Arkema will be able to provide more differentiated, reliable supplies to Korean customers.
Beyond its role in Korea, this project marks an important step in Arkema's strategy to further develop the GAA market in Northeast Asia. By adding a local storage node to its regional supply network, Arkema will strengthen the connection between regional supply capabilities, logistics and market operations, supporting a more integrated supply setup for the region.
Hervé Castres Saint Martin, Group President for Acrylic Monomers at Arkema, said: "Asia is a key region in Arkema's global acrylics footprint. This project in Korea further strengthens our regional synergies across Northeast Asia and better connects our production, supply and logistics networks. By bringing us closer to our Korean customers, it will also enable our regional footprint to better support customer-driven application development and collaborative innovation. This project reflects our long-term commitment to deepening our presence in Asia, enhancing regional supply resilience, and driving business growth through innovation and sustainability." 
Arkema is one of the world's major producers of acrylic monomers. Supported by its production site in Taixing, China, Arkema's acrylic business in Asia plays a key role in the Group's regional operations, serving markets across China, Japan, Korea and Southeast Asia. Alongside strengthening its regional presence, Arkema is also advancing sustainability initiatives across its acrylic value chain, including ISCC+ Mass Balance certification across all of its acrylic monomer production sites worldwide, further supporting customers seeking lower-carbon and more circular materials solutions.
Building on its unique set of expertise in materials science, Arkema offers a portfolio of first-class technologies to address ever-growing demand for new and more sustainable materials. With the ambition to become a world leader in Specialty Materials, the Group is structured into three complementary, resilient and highly innovative segments dedicated to Specialty Materials - Adhesive Solutions, Advanced Materials, and Coating Solutions - accounting for some 85% of Group sales in 2025, and a Primary Materials segment regrouping well-positioned large scale industrials activities. Arkema offers cutting-edge technological solutions to meet the challenges of, among other things, new energies, access to water, recycling, urbanization and mobility, and fosters a permanent dialogue with all its stakeholders. The Group reported sales of around €9.1 billion in 2025 and operates in some 55 countries with 20,700 employees worldwide.

Mkango Resources to Change Name to Mkango Magnetic Materials on 23 September
Fiona Craig 
21 September 2026 2 min read 
MKA.V 
Rare earth minerals ©Peggy Greb, US department of agriculture Mkango Resources (LSE:MKA) has announced that it will change its name to Mkango Magnetic Materials Limited from the start of trading on 23 September 2026, reflecting its increasing focus on rare earth magnet manufacturing and recycling. 
The company, which is listed on AIM and the TSX Venture Exchange, confirmed that its trading symbol will remain MKA on both exchanges. Existing shareholder arrangements will also remain unchanged. 
The name change reflects Mkango's strategy of expanding its downstream rare earth activities, including the production of recycled magnets, alloys and oxides, alongside its existing mining and processing projects. 
Through its majority-owned subsidiary Maginito, the company is developing a rare earth magnet recycling and manufacturing business with operations in the United Kingdom, Germany and the United States. 
Its portfolio includes the Remloy business in Germany and HyProMag operations in the UK and Germany. The company is also expanding its Hydrogen Processing of Magnet Scrap (HPMS) recycling technology into the US through the HyProMag USA joint venture. 
These operations cover different stages of magnet recycling and manufacturing, including short-, medium- and long-loop recycling processes. 
Mkango's downstream activities focus on recovering and processing rare earth elements, including neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium and terbium, which are used in permanent magnets for applications such as electric vehicles, wind turbines and other clean energy technologies. 
The company also continues to advance its upstream rare earth interests, including the Songwe Hill project in Malawi and the proposed Pulawy rare earth separation plant in Poland. 
Both projects have been designated Strategic Projects under the European Union's Critical Raw Materials Act and have received US development funding for front-end engineering and design activities. 
Mkango is also pursuing a proposed NASDAQ listing of these assets through a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) merger involving Mkango Rare Earths Limited. 
The planned name change does not alter the company's existing exchange listings or trading symbol. It reflects the group's strategy of developing its rare earth magnet recycling and manufacturing operations while continuing work on its mining and processing assets.

How 60 GHz Radar Improves Low-Power Presence Sensing In IoT Devices
Track occupancy and motion continuously without keeping the full sensing and processing chain active.
September 21st, 2026 - 
By: Chris Wengerter 
Battery-powered IoT devices must maintain room-level awareness without keeping their full sensing and processing chains continuously active. A duty-cycled architecture built around sensors that detect larger body motion and micro-motion allows smart thermostats, occupancy sensors, and security systems to monitor occupancy, track motion, and wake downstream hardware only when needed.
This article reviews how 60 GHz frequency-modulated continuous-wave radar supports low-power presence sensing in IoT designs. It uses Infineon’s XENSIV BGT60CUTR13AIP as an implementation example of antenna-in-package (AIP) integration, on-chip radar processing, and autonomous low-power operation for occupancy and motion detection without continuous host-side processing.
Sensor limitations in low-power presence detection
Passive infrared (PIR) sensors detect changes in infrared radiation as a person moves relative to the sensor. Low power draw and low cost explain their widespread use in occupancy devices, yet PIR output is limited to simple binary motion events with no range, angle, or fine-movement data. Dependence on thermal contrast also creates false-trigger risk and causes missed occupancy when people remain stationary. PIR sensors also require a clear field of view through an infrared-transparent window or lens, which constrains sensor placement and enclosure design.
In applications such as video doorbells and security cameras, the camera performs the product’s primary imaging function. After a low-power sensor triggers system wake-up, the camera provides visual verification and richer scene context. However, using the camera for continuous presence detection keeps the image sensor, host processor, memory, and image-processing pipeline active and increases average current in battery-powered products. Cameras also require optical windows, clear fields of view, and adequate illumination. These requirements limit mechanical design flexibility.
Ultrasonic sensing provides a non-optical option for proximity detection, though acoustic noise, airflow, temperature variation, and material reflections degrade sensor performance. Spatial detail is also limited, reducing the sensor’s ability to detect fine motion or separate occupants and objects by range.
These constraints shift low-power presence sensing from component selection to system architecture. Designers need an always-available sensing front end that detects occupancy and motion without keeping higher-power sensing, processing, or imaging blocks active.
FMCW radar as an active sensing method
A 60 GHz-band frequency-modulated continuous-wave radar provides the required front end for accurate, low-power presence sensing by using RF measurement instead of thermal contrast, optical imaging, or acoustic propagation. The transmitter emits a continuous waveform whose frequency sweeps over time. Reflections from people and objects return to the receiver, where differences between transmitted and received signals provide range and motion information.
For compact IoT devices, 60 GHz operation reduces antenna dimensions, while wide FMCW bandwidth provides fine range resolution for short-range indoor sensing. FMCW sensing also supports occupancy detection after larger body motion stops, as breathing, posture shifts, and other micro-motion create measurable changes in the returned signal. These signal changes allow radar to detect presence when motion-only sensors no longer register movement.
RF sensing further reduces dependence on environmental conditions that affect PIR, camera, and ultrasonic sensors. Operation in darkness, bright sunlight, smoke, or steam, along with placement behind RF-transparent or low-loss enclosure materials, gives designers more flexibility in enclosure design and sensor placement.
Infineon’s XENSIV BGT60CUTR13AIP implements this sensing model as a 57 to 64 GHz CMOS radar sensor with 7 GHz FMCW bandwidth. With a detection range of approximately 0.025 m to 20 m, the sensor covers close interaction sensing and room-scale occupancy detection. 
Integrated radar architecture for compact IoT designs
The BGT60CUTR13AIP combines the radar monolithic microwave integrated circuit (MMIC), antenna structures, internal low-dropout regulators, an oscillator, and control logic in a compact antenna-in-package device measuring approximately 6.05 mm × 4.3 mm × 0.9 mm.
Moving the antennas and support circuitry into the package reduces external RF structures, controlled RF routing, antenna placement, and board-level tuning required in discrete radar designs. Integration also minimizes external component count, simplifies the bill of materials (BOM), limits always-connected components that add standby current, and improves design repeatability in space-constrained IoT products.
The AIP design integrates one transmit antenna and three receive antennas in an L-shaped array for azimuth and elevation sensing. This layout provides a field of view up to 150 degrees in both azimuth and elevation, enabling room-scale presence sensing from wall-mounted, ceiling-mounted, or embedded product locations.
On-chip processing and host-MCU wake-up
On-chip processing extends integration from the RF front end to signal analysis. By shifting radar processing from the host MCU to the sensor, the BGT60CUTR13AIP reduces continuous host-side processing of the radar data stream.
An integrated hardware accelerator handles computationally demanding radar functions, including 2D fast Fourier transforms (FFTs), filtering, constant false alarm rate (CFAR) processing, and angle-of-arrival estimation. A moving-target indication (MTI) function supports autonomous motion detection. When the radar identifies relevant activity, an interrupt wakes the host MCU to execute higher-level application logic.
Partitioning keeps environmental monitoring on the radar front end while reserving the host system for application logic, wireless communication, display control, camera activation, or cloud interaction. Host-level processing occurs only when a radar-detected event warrants a system response.
System power benefits of radar-triggered operation
An event-triggered model reduces average current by limiting how long higher-power subsystems remain active between events. Keeping the MCU, camera, display, or radio awake increases power consumption even when each component has efficient active-mode specifications.
Low-power radar changes the system duty-cycle profile by keeping an always-available sensing front end active while higher-power subsystems remain off or in low-power standby. The BGT60CUTR13AIP supports sensing modes below 1 mW and deep-sleep operation around 0.1 mW, allowing activity monitoring without full-system operation.
In a security-camera architecture, radar functions as a first-stage trigger. The sensor monitors for presence or movement in a defined region, then activates image capture only when the event requires imaging. This reduces unnecessary processing, heat generation, and data capture during idle periods.
Radar-triggered operation also extends to displays, thermostats, occupancy sensors, and lighting controls, allowing these systems to respond to presence or proximity without continuous host-side processing.
Applications in smart home and building systems
Radar-based presence sensing enables smart home and building devices that require more detailed occupancy context than a binary motion event. In lighting and HVAC systems, micro-motion detection helps prevent false vacancy decisions when occupants remain still and allows control algorithms to differentiate empty rooms from quietly occupied spaces.
In consumer electronics, radar supports proximity-aware operation without optical capture. Smart TVs, monitors, speakers, and displays use proximity data to respond as people enter a room, approach the device, or leave the space while avoiding continuous image sensing.
Security applications use radar as a presence-aware front end for imaging, transmission, or recording functions, activating higher-power subsystems only after motion or presence is detected in a defined region.
More advanced implementations, such as room activity classification, gesture-based controls, and vital-sign monitoring, extend radar sensing beyond occupancy detection. Each use case requires application-specific firmware, placement, and validation, yet the sensing architecture remains consistent: low-power radar delivers local perception without continuous image capture or host-side processing.
Development and integration considerations
Adding RF sensing to compact IoT products introduces antenna, layout, regulatory, and test requirements. Infineon supports these requirements through the BGT60CUTR13AIP’s antenna-in-package design, FCC-certified reference designs, and developer resources. The integrated antenna structure reduces RF layout complexity while giving teams a validated starting point for product development.
Mechanical integration of presence-sensing devices benefits from radar placement behind RF-transparent or low-loss enclosure materials. Unlike cameras and PIR sensors, radar does not require a lens, optical window, or visible aperture, supporting sealed housings and discreet placement in residential and workplace environments.
Beyond mechanical design, Infineon provides ModusToolbox software tools , evaluation kits, and documentation for IoT use cases. These resources support prototyping, validation, and firmware partitioning between the radar sensor and host MCU while helping teams coordinate RF design, enclosure integration, and application development.
Conclusion
Reliable IoT presence detection requires a sensing front end that tracks occupancy and motion continuously without keeping the full sensing and processing chain active. PIR, camera, and ultrasonic sensors impose tradeoffs in spatial coverage, power draw, optical access, and environmental sensitivity that limit their use as always-on solutions in battery-powered designs.
Infineon’s XENSIV BGT60CUTR13AIP 60 GHz CMOS radar sensor combines FMCW sensing, 7 GHz bandwidth, antenna-in-package integration, on-chip acceleration, and autonomous host-MCU wake-up to support local occupancy awareness without continuous full-system operation. For smart home, smart building, security, display, and battery-powered sensing designs, this 60 GHz radar architecture provides a compact front end for more reliable presence detection within constrained power and space budgets.

ABB’s new direct current portfolio aims to rewire AI data center energy infrastructure
Group press release
ABB introduces Infinitus, the industry’s first source-to-rack direct current portfolio for AI data centers designed for architecture flexibility
Breakthrough Infinitus solid-state transformers help maximize energy efficiency and reduce physical footprint, alongside DC power distribution and protection technologies to enhance overall system performance
Infinitus direct current portfolio expected to drive similar benefits across other industries including industrial buildings, manufacturing, renewables, and marine operations
ABB today announced the launch of Infinitus, a portfolio of direct current (DC) solutions designed to manage the increasing power demands of AI data centers. The portfolio will accelerate the adoption of DC architectures in data centers improving energy efficiency and reducing power infrastructure footprint, while increasing available computing capacity. ABB expects other energy-intensive industries to make the same transition.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) expects global data center electricity demand to more than double by 2030 and ABB estimates that approximately 25-40% of new capacity installed in 2030 could be using DC distribution. Next-generation AI chips are expected to draw 1 MW per rack and beyond, an increase from today's almost 200 kW, requiring a shift to DC architecture that can support performance while driving energy efficiency. With 800 VDC distribution, the footprint is more compact while eliminating redundant conversion steps and cutting heat losses of conventional alternating current (AC) systems. A recent BCG / ABB report calculated that DC distribution delivers energy efficiency gains of more than 5% and increases available space for compute racks. For a 500MW data center, a 5% efficiency gain can mean 25 MW more power for revenue-generating IT loads and more than US $300 million in potential additional revenue per year. With 5% efficiency gains for a 500 MW data center campus, the energy savings over one year would be equivalent to powering Washington D.C. for almost a full week.
Giampiero Frisio, President of ABB’s Electrification business area, said: “ABB has pioneered DC technology for more than 25 years across several segments. We are working closely with chipmakers, hyperscale customers, supply partners and industry bodies to set the standards and the pace for the roll-out of high-efficiency DC architectures. Infinitus is the first portfolio providing the building blocks for any data center architecture - either DC native or hybrid AC/ DC - to power next-generation AI chips efficiently. This technology will bring similar energy efficiency gains to other energy-intensive industries such as large scale manufacturing, renewables and marine operations.”
Infinitus is the industry's first integrated source-to-rack DC portfolio. At its core is ABB’s breakthrough Infinitus solid-state transformer technology, enabling sites to operate with a smaller footprint and greater energy efficiency. As the only major electrification supplier with both the world's first fully IEC-certified solid-state circuit breaker and an industry-first static medium-voltage UPS in production, ABB delivers a breadth of technology unmatched in the market.
ABB’s Infinitus DC portfolio includes five key building blocks:
Medium Voltage Powertrains deliver stable resilient power from the grid or on-site generation;
DC Sources and Power Quality converts AC to DC removing conversion from white space;
DC Power Distribution delivers power safely and reliably, enabling higher power density in a smaller footprint;
DC Power Protection provides protection for operators, AI servers and hardware from DC overcurrents;
Cooling Optimization reduces energy consumption across grey and white space with DC connected variable speed drives and motors.
ABB works with customers to design solutions tailored to their specific power demands, facility layout, and energy mix. This partnership approach ensures each deployment is optimized for maximum efficiency and reliability. The Infinitus portfolio complements traditional AC systems with DC flexibility that supports customers across all power architectures while also enabling unprecedented efficiency, reliability, and scalability for AI-era data centers.
For next-generation data centers, this integrated architecture enables the high-density, high-efficiency power delivery that future AI chips demand. With a number of main components produced in the next twelve months, the first DC-native facilities using the complete Infinitus portfolio are expected to be installed and operational within two to three years.
The portfolio launch extends support for ABB's continued collaboration with NVIDIA, first announced in October 2025, to develop 800 VDC power architectures for gigawatt-scale AI facilities. ABB brings more than 25 years of DC experience and over 700 patents spanning renewables, power generation, energy storage, motors and drives.
ABB is a global technology leader in electrification and automation, enabling a more sustainable and resource-efficient future. By connecting its engineering and digitalization expertise, ABB helps industries run at high performance, while becoming more efficient, productive and sustainable so they outperform. At ABB, we call this ‘Engineered to Outrun’. The company has over 140 years of history and around 110,000 employees worldwide. ABB’s shares are listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange (ABBN) and Nasdaq Stockholm (ABB). www.abb.com

Tata Electronics, Sumitomo Chemical sign MoU to strengthen semiconductor supply chain
By Nitisha Dubey 
Share
Facebook
X

September 21, 2026 
Tata Electronics is building India’s first commercial 12-inch (300 mm) semiconductor Fab in Dholera 
Tata Electronics has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Japan-based Sumitomo Chemical to strengthen India’s semiconductor materials supply chain and support the development of a domestic semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem.
Under the agreement, the companies will explore a collaboration under which Sumitomo Chemical will supply semiconductor materials to Tata Electronics’ upcoming semiconductor Fab in Dholera, Gujarat. The materials will include photoresists, functional chemicals and high-purity chemicals such as hydrogen peroxide, isopropyl alcohol, ammonia water and sulfuric acid.
The two companies will also explore the manufacturing of semiconductor materials and high-purity chemicals in India, with Tata Electronics supporting Sumitomo Chemical in evaluating opportunities for local production.
Dr. Randhir Thakur, CEO and MD, Tata Electronics, said the partnership would help strengthen the supply of high-quality materials for the company’s upcoming Fab while contributing to India-Japan cooperation in the semiconductor sector.
- Advertisement - 
Satoshi Honda, Managing Executive Officer, Sumitomo Chemical, said the company aims to contribute to a stable supply of semiconductor materials and a more diversified semiconductor supply chain in India by leveraging its expertise in photoresists, functional chemicals and high-purity chemicals.
Tata Electronics is building India’s first commercial 12-inch (300 mm) semiconductor Fab in Dholera, Gujarat, with a planned investment of $11 billion. The facility is expected to manufacture chips for applications including automotive, mobile devices and artificial intelligence.
The company has also partnered with Taiwan’s PSMC to gain access to semiconductor technologies spanning 28nm to 110nm nodes. The partnership with Sumitomo Chemical is expected to further strengthen the Fab’s supply ecosystem by adding capabilities across semiconductor materials and high-purity chemicals.
The collaboration comes as India works to build a more diversified and resilient semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem, with domestic capabilities in materials, equipment, manufacturing, process technologies and chip design.

Most Qorvo (QRVO) Bondholders Said Yes, but Skyworks (SWKS) Is Still Waiting
Maham Fatima 
September 21, 2026 3 min read 
SWKS 
+0.21% 
QRVO 
0.00% 
On September 18, Skyworks Solutions (NASDAQ: SWKS ) extended the deadline on its offers to swap Qorvo (NASDAQ: QRVO ) bonds for new Skyworks debt, moving it to September 25. Bondholders are hardly balking. But the swap cannot settle until the Qorvo merger closes, so the real story is timing, and a routine bond notice turns out to be a decent window into how the whole combination is going. 
Hut 8 (HUT) Has $26.6B in Leases, but Where Is the Revenue? Bondholders Have Already Signed On 
Begin with the people lending to the other side of this deal. By the September 18 cutoff, holders had tendered $775,664,000 of Qorvo's 2029 notes, or 91.25% of what is outstanding. The 2031 series did even better, at 93.33%. That is close to a full vote for swapping into Skyworks paper. Anyone who has already tendered does not have to lift a finger, while latecomers can still join until September 25. 
The operating business is also holding up. On July 28, Skyworks reported third-quarter revenue of $935 million for a quarter that ended July 3, ahead of expectations. Automotive and data center posted double-digit gains, and management says it added design wins in telematics, infotainment, and AI data center switches. Looking ahead, the September quarter is guided to $1.01 billion to $1.06 billion in revenue, helped by a high-teens sequential jump in mobile as its largest customer launches new products. 
Another Extension, No Guarantees 
The first problem is that the finish line keeps moving. Skyworks says regulatory approvals are progressing, not done, and it warns there is no assurance the closing arrives on schedule. The bond swap cannot settle until no sooner than two business days after the merger closes, so every slip in the deal means another extension notice like this one. 
The price of getting there is real, too. Skyworks expects to raise about $2 billion of acquisition debt, and its September quarter outlook already absorbs about $0.03 a share of added interest expense for just a partial quarter. In the same July 28 release, it decided to stop declaring quarterly dividends and replaced a buyback program due to expire in February 2027 with a new $2 billion one that carries no minimum purchase requirement. Shareholders who wanted an income stream lose it. And GAAP earnings of $0.22 a share sit far below the $1.08 in adjusted earnings, so the adjusted figure strips out a lot. 
Skeptics Crowd the Stock 
35 hedge funds owned Skyworks in the latest quarter, the same 35 as before, so big money is neither piling in nor leaving. Short interest is the louder signal, at 36.38% of the float, which is heavy skepticism. Crowded shorts can fuel a sharp rally if the news turns, though some of this may be hedging rather than pure conviction. At a forward P/E of 17.61, as of September 18, the price is not demanding, so the skepticism is hard to pin on a rich valuation. 
Story Continues 
Hope Meets the Closing Date 
Skyworks is asking the market to look past a delay and trust a closing date it cannot guarantee. Bondholders have made their choice, while short sellers are betting the other way. The answer will come from whether Qorvo's regulatory approvals arrive in time for a close by year-end. If they do, and automotive and data center keep growing, the bulls get a bigger, better-funded company. If the deadline slips again or the interest bill runs heavier than guided, the bears get their case.

Hexagon and GelSight Integrate Portable Dimensional and Surface Inspection 
September 21, 2026 
Hexagon has announced an expanded integration with GelSight , building on the companies’ global partnership first announced in 2024. The new workflow connects the Hexagon Absolute Arm , GelSight Mobile Series 2 and VGMETROLOGY Essential software, giving manufacturers a single environment to capture, align and analyze dimensional and high-resolution surface inspection data.
Manufacturers often rely on separate technologies to understand a part’s geometry and its small surface defects, requiring inspection results to be reviewed and reconciled independently. The new workflow addresses this by bringing those results into a common coordinate system: an optical scan from the Absolute Arm establishes the part’s geometry, GelSight Mobile Series 2 captures high-resolution surface measurements at specific areas of interest, and VGMETROLOGY Essential brings the data together, allowing surface findings to be visualized in context with the broader scan and incorporated into a single analysis and reporting workflow.
“Manufacturers have never lacked for inspection data. The challenge has always been bringing it together in a way that’s easy to act on,” said Brian Winters, Product Manager for the Absolute Arm at Hexagon Manufacturing Intelligence. “ Connecting the Absolute Arm with GelSight’s surface measurements inside VGMETROLOGY gives quality teams one place to see the whole part, geometry and surface detail together, and that’s a meaningful step toward inspection that fits into the production process rather than sitting outside of it.” 
More Complete View of the Part 
The integrated workflow gives manufacturers several practical advantages:
See a More Complete Digital Twin. The workflow combines dimensional and high-resolution surface information within one inspection process, rather than treating them as separate steps.
Detect Smaller Imperfections. GelSight provides approximately 1-micron Z resolution, allowing manufacturers to identify surface defects that traditional 3D scanning may not reliably capture.
Put Defects in Context. Detailed surface measurements are connected to their precise location on the overall component, rather than analyzed in isolation.
Bring Inspection Data Together. VGMETROLOGY Essential connects GelSight surface measurements with Absolute Arm scan data, providing a consolidated environment to visualize, analyze and report inspection results.
Simplify Reporting. Bringing inspection data into a common coordinate system can reduce the manual effort required to document multiple inspection locations and communicate findings.
Bring Inspection Closer to Production. In one aerospace application, the workflow reduced a three-day external analysis process by bringing the capability directly to the shop floor.
VGMETROLOGY delivers comprehensive, high-precision measurement tools for CT data, CAD models, meshes, and point clouds. Full GD&T compliance, easy-to-use multipart functionality, smart pattern logic and integrated statistical process control allow users to do robust metrology with ease.
“Since our partnership with Hexagon began in 2024, we’ve focused on making GelSight’s surface data useful in the context of the full part, not just as a standalone measurement,” said Youssef Benmokhtar, CEO, GelSight. “ When a defect is tied directly to its location on the component, it stops being an isolated data point and becomes something a quality team can immediately locate, understand and act on.” 
For more information: www.hexagon.com

title: Onsemi to Eliminate Power Module Assembly by Integrating Chips Into Wafers - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media
source: Google News: THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media
publisher: THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media
query: "onsemi" (Korea OR Korean) after:2026-09-01 before:2026-10-01
content_text:
Onsemi has unveiled a new technology that uses silicon wafers as substrates for power semiconductor packages, integrating power semiconductors and control chips into a single structure to make power systems smaller and more efficient.
​Onsemi on Sept. 18 unveiled its Embedded Power Platform (EPP).
​EPP is similar in concept to embedded-die technology, which places power semiconductor chips inside a package substrate. The difference is that EPP uses a 12-inch silicon wafer as the package substrate instead of a conventional printed circuit board (PCB).
​Conventional power modules mount multiple power semiconductor chips on a substrate and connect them with metal wires. EPP integrates multiple chips, including silicon (Si), silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) power semiconductors, as well as drivers and controllers, directly onto a wafer.
​Onsemi said the architecture can increase power density by three to five times compared with existing solutions. Shorter connections between chips reduce power losses caused by current flow and voltage fluctuations generated during switching. The company also said the use of silicon, which has high thermal conductivity, improves heat dissipation.
​Key applications include traction inverters for electric vehicles and artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.
​A traction inverter converts direct-current electricity from a battery into alternating-current electricity used to drive a motor. Onsemi said EPP can increase inverter power density by up to four times and reduce power losses by 15%.
​Another feature is that a single basic architecture can be used across different power ratings. Automakers would not need to develop separate inverters for entry-level and high-performance vehicles. Onsemi said this could shorten development time by up to four months.
​Onsemi said Japanese automaker Subaru is participating as an early partner for EPP. Subaru will receive engineering samples and simulation models from Onsemi and evaluate whether EPP can be applied to future electrified vehicles.
​The company said applying EPP to solid-state circuit breakers for AI data centers could reduce product size by 50% and lower operating temperatures by 20%.
​"Semiconductors and packages have been treated as separate technologies for decades," said Hassane El-Khoury, president and CEO of Onsemi. "EPP integrates silicon itself as part of the system architecture."
​Onsemi plans to begin supplying EPP samples to key customers in the automotive and AI sectors this year.

content_text:
Charles River Community Health launches $5.2M expansion to meet high patient demand 
By Sherry Keyles 
● 
Community 
● 
September 20, 2026 
With nearly 10% of Waltham residents turning to Charles River Community Health for essential medical care, the health center is launching a major expansion at its Foundry Avenue location to meet the city’s growing healthcare needs. 
The project, expected to be completed by June 30, 2027, will increase the health center’s space from 12,000 to 17,000 square feet, expanding capacity in all departments and adding vision care to the center’s offerings. 
“Waltham is actually our single largest concentration of patients across any town or city we serve,” CRCH CEO Matthew Mullaney said. “In 2025 alone, we served 5,465 patients from Waltham’s three zip codes, roughly 10% of the city.”
CRCH CEO Matt Mullaney (right) with State Representative Thomas M. Stanley last year. Photo courtesy Matt Mullaney. 
Construction is scheduled to begin in November or December. Affinia Therapeutics occupied the new space until a few weeks ago.
Mullaney said the build-out will not only introduce vision care but also add six medical exam rooms (a 30% increase), three behavioral health rooms (doubling current capacity), two dental operatories (a 40% increase) and a new nursing station. 
“Our goal is to be one-stop shopping,” Mullaney said.
He estimates the new square footage will allow the health center to accommodate an additional 3,000 to 4,000 medical patients once fully operational. Currently, the center has wait lists in all departments and nonurgent appointment waits of over three weeks for established patients.
“We’re seeing some of our longest wait times for primary care right here in Waltham,” said Mullaney. “We have longer waiting lists for dental in Waltham. We have five dental operatories right now, and in Brighton we have 12.
“It turns out even though the health center was started here in the Allston/Brighton area, the center of gravity has really moved to Waltham,” Mullaney added. 
The health center opened in Waltham in 2004 after Waltham Hospital closed, and moved to its current location at 43 Foundry Ave. in 2018. 
Advertisement 
The total cost for the Waltham expansion is estimated at $5.2 million. To fund the work, the health center is mounting a fundraising campaign targeting at least $3.5 million. 
Architectural floor plan illustrating the planned $5.2M expansion of the Charles River Community Health facility in Waltham. Provided by: Matthew Mullaney. 
CRCH, which also operates a site in Brighton, is the only federally qualified health center serving Waltham, Watertown, Brighton and Allston. In its two locations, the health center cares for more than 14,000 individuals. 
Serving medically underserved areas and populations, FQHCs are federally funded nonprofits statutorily required to provide primary care for everyone, regardless of ability to pay. 
CRCH is also an active member of the Community Care Alliance, maintaining affiliations with Beth Israel Lahey Health (including Mount Auburn Hospital and BIDMC) and Boston Children’s Hospital to coordinate affordable specialty and acute care.
Preparing for Medicaid Changes 
The expansion comes as community health centers across Massachusetts brace for changes to federal Medicaid policies that could leave thousands of state residents without insurance coverage on Jan. 1, 2027. 
Mullaney said that while the expansion is not driven solely by the Medicaid changes, CRCH stands ready to help patients who currently have MassHealth coverage.
“We are opening this new space so we can better serve our community, from longtime residents to new arrivals, no matter what insurance they have or whether they need our help getting and keeping coverage as Medicaid policies shift in 2027,” he said. “We have a health benefit department and community health workers who are becoming more and more knowledgeable about some of the insurance changes.
“So the most important thing we’re doing is getting smart about what’s coming and how that’s going to work so that we could give people good advice,” Mullaney said. “Hopefully, make them feel more informed, calm and less worried about their insurance.”
Serving the Diverse Community 
Mullaney said CRCH staff work directly with uninsured patients to help them enroll in coverage or access care.
“We’re actually one of the places in the commonwealth where you can have Health Safety Net and get care. You can’t just go anywhere with that type of insurance,” he said, adding that the center also sees patients with other types of insurance including Medicare and commercial plans. 
CRHC’s demographic reflects Waltham’s diversity. Mullaney said most current patients are first-, second- and third-generation immigrants, with two-thirds identifying as Latino. Most patients receive healthcare services in languages other than English. According to CRHC’s 2025 annual report , 98% of patients live at or below 200% of the federal poverty level of $64,300/year for a family of four. 
“In my opinion, we work really hard to be a welcoming place for people from all backgrounds,” Mullaney said when asked what sets CRHC apart from other community health centers. “It’s a place where people feel welcome and not judged.” 
CRCH will discuss the expansion at its fall breakfast on Sept. 29 at Gore Place from 7:30 to 9 a.m. The guest speaker is Beth Israel Lahey Health Chief Community and Health Impact Officer Juan Fernando Lopera, who will talk about his experience as an immigrant, a patient and a health system leader. 
Tickets are $25, and you can register online through the health center’s website .

content_text:
The Airbus A380 got a second life. Here's where you can still fly on the world's largest passenger jet.
By 
Pete Syme 
You're currently following this author!
Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.
Follow 
Emirates is the biggest operator of the world's largest passenger jet. 
Bloomberg/Getty Images 
2026-09-20T09:29:39.653Z
