content_text:
Chemours, DuPont, Corteva reach $590M settlement with NC over PFAS lawsuits
By Lily Carey 
Updated September 10, 2026 5:10 PM 
Key Takeaways
AI-generated summary reviewed by our newsroom.
Read our AI Policy. 
Chemours, Corteva, and DuPont reached a $590 million PFAS settlement in NC.
The deal sends $380 million to 11 local authorities hit by PFAS pollution.
DuPont and Corteva will create a $135 million reserve fund for ongoing work.
The three chemical companies that dumped forever chemicals into North Carolina’s rivers for decades have reached a $590 million settlement to resolve several lawsuits in the state.
The settlement, announced Thursday, is the “largest state environmental damages recovery in North Carolina history,” N.C. Attorney General Jeff Jackson said Thursday. It also resolves a state lawsuit against the three companies — Chemours, DuPont and Corteva — that’s dragged on since 2020.
“Roughly 3.5 million North Carolinians currently drink water with PFAS levels above federal health standards in drinking water,” said Reid Wilson, secretary of the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality. “That’s one out of every three people in this state, and this is not just numbers; these are people and families and communities. So this is a really urgent issue because everyone expects and deserves that when they turn on the tap, they’re going to get clean, healthy drinking water.”
North Carolina has been seeking damages from the three companies since 2016, when officials discovered that Chemours had been knowingly discharging forever chemicals, known as PFAS, from its Fayetteville Works industrial plant in Cumberland County and into the Cape Fear River. Drinking water contaminated with PFAS can lead to cancers and developmental issues; the chemicals are extremely difficult to filter from water, and can remain in the human body indefinitely.
The N.C. DEQ had secured a $1.2 billion consent order against Chemours in 2019, and part of Thursday’s settlement will require DuPont, Chemours’ former parent company, to continue funding the cleanup and well testing efforts that started under that consent order if Chemours goes bankrupt.
DuPont had owned the plant since the 1970s before spinning Chemours out into its own company in 2015, but DuPont and Corteva, another one of its offshoots, are still legally liable for pollution at the Fayetteville plant.
Work continues on container tanks at the Chemours plant in a file photo from Nov. 28, 2018. The tanks were installed as measures to reduce PFAS emissions. Melissa Sue Gerrits Carolina Public Press 
What’s in the $590M settlement
Under the settlement, Chemours, DuPont and Corteva will pay a total of $455 million to North Carolina authorities over the next 15 years. $380 million will be paid to 11 local authorities that were impacted by the companies’ PFAS pollution, while another $75 million will be paid to the state. Chemours will pay for half of the $455 million, and DuPont and Corteva will pay the other half.
On top of that, DuPont will also establish a $135 million reserve fund. That’s because Chemours, which was spun out of DuPont in 2015, faces a “real risk of bankruptcy,” Jackson said.
If Chemours does go bankrupt, that reserve fund will act as a “backstop” to make sure that DuPont can cover the full costs of the 2019 consent order, Wilson said.
While it’s not immediately clear what the money will be used for, money from the 2019 consent order has been used to install water treatment systems, sample residential wells, and install pollution control technology and a physical barrier wall at Fayetteville Works.
A spokesperson for Jackson told The N&O that the state will use $55 million of its $75 million from this settlement for the new Emerging Contaminant Mitigation Fund that was created this year by state lawmakers.
The 11 local authorities getting settlement payments are Bladen, Brunswick, Columbus, Cumberland, New Hanover, Robeson and Sampson counties, and the Town of Wrightsville Beach, City of Lumberton, Village of Bald Head Island and Lower Cape Fear Water and Sewer Authority.
After EPA settlement, leaders say NC deal is stronger
Thursday’s announcement comes just over two months after the EPA and the federal Department of Justice reached their own $450 million settlement with Chemours — a deal that North Carolina leaders decried as being too weak.
The EPA settlement, announced in June, resolved lawsuits over Chemours’ PFAS pollution in Fayetteville, as well as at other plants in New Jersey and West Virginia. But while federal officials pegged the settlement at $450 million, North Carolina will only end up receiving an estimated $2 million annually from that deal for the next 15 years, Jackson said Thursday.
“We were hoping that the EPA would take this seriously, but they failed,” Jackson said. “They did a slap on the wrist for... DuPont and Chemours. That was unacceptable. We knew we were going to have to take the lead.”
Chemours told The N&O last month that it was giving less money to North Carolina in the EPA settlement because it already had existing cleanup efforts in the state. Jackson, Gov. Josh Stein and other state leaders pointed to the settlement as a sign that the EPA was less willing to hold polluters like Chemours accountable under the leadership of Trump appointee Lee Zeldin.
Local cleanup, Chemours expansion still lie ahead
While Thursday’s settlement holds Chemours accountable, it’s “not the end of the story,” said Jean Zhuang, an attorney for the Southern Environmental Law Center.
Chemours is still planning an expansion of its Fayetteville Works plant, and while the state has taken steps to curb PFAS pollution at the plant, it hasn’t stopped it entirely.
“While this settlement would help clean up existing pollution, we have to stop the tap ... and part of that means denying the permit for Chemours’ expansion,” said Cori Bell, a senior attorney for the Natural Resources Defense Council.
When asked about the expansion, Wilson told The N&O Thursday that the DEQ “[does] not currently have a pending application from Chemours for... an air quality permit to expand their operations.” According to DEQ’s website, Chemours has submitted an application for a new air quality permit, but DEQ had deemed their application incomplete, and has not received a full application.
DEQ still maintains its full permitting authority under the settlement, Wilson noted — in other words, they can still deny Chemours’ air quality permit expansion if they want to.
Zhuang also said that while this settlement gives “a significant amount of funds for local municipalities who might need it,” the $380 million divided among the 11 local authorities may not be enough to fully clean up PFAS pollution hotspots.
Cleaning up polluted water systems and piping in clean water supply can be an expensive task. Thursday’s news conference took place at the Gray’s Creek Water Project in Cumberland County, which is delivering clean water to two elementary schools and “more than 200 to 300 homes” directly near the Fayetteville Works plant, according to Cumberland County executive Kirk deViere. A sign at the Gray’s Creek site showed that the EPA provided over $9 million for the project.
For local leaders, the next step is taking PFAS control efforts “from the courtroom to the community,” deViere said Thursday.

Lonza to build large-scale spray-drying facility in Oregon
September 10, 2026 | By Mary Bailey 
Lonza , Group AG (Basel, Switzerland) announced plans to further strengthen its significant U.S. presence by constructing a large-scale commercial spray-drying facility in Bend, Oregon. The investment will establish Lonza as the leading contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) provider of commercial-scale spray-dried dispersion (SDD) PSD-4 capacity in the U.S. Lonza will offer a full range of SDD capacity to support customers across both clinical and commercial programs. Through its integrated end-to-end offering, Lonza will support the development and manufacturing of small molecules and other modalities, including biologics and mRNA.
SDD technologies are increasingly relevant in modern drug development, as the industry addresses the growing complexity of molecules and their related bioavailability challenges. The demand for SDD CDMO services has grown alongside the increasing scientific complexity of pharmaceutical pipelines, driven by the increasing prevalence of poorly soluble drug substances. Today, a significant share of molecules in the clinical pipeline requires bioavailability enhancement. The Bend expansion is intended to meet this growing market demand, with a particular focus on U.S. demand, enabling Lonza to provide customers with an additional option to access a complete and integrated end-to-end development and manufacturing solution for SDDs.
Wolfgang Wienand, Chief Executive Officer, Lonza, said: “The investment in the Bend site reflects our conviction that the United States will remain a leading source of pharmaceutical innovation and a key market for Lonza. It also delivers on our One Lonza strategy, powered by the Lonza Engine, to invest where we can create the greatest value for our customers and, ultimately, for patients. By significantly expanding our commercial-scale spray-drying capabilities, we strengthen a technology that can fundamentally improve the delivery and bioavailability of medicines. With this, our world-class particle engineering team in Bend will be even better able to support our customers in turning their breakthrough innovations into viable products and to manufacture the medicines of tomorrow.”
Christian Seufert, Head of Advanced Synthesis, Lonza, added: “The growing number of complex drug molecules is increasing demand for advanced particle engineering technologies. With decades of expertise in spray-drying, our Bend team helps customers address formulation challenges and progress their programs efficiently. This investment expands the capacity and capabilities needed to support customers from development through commercialization.”
The new facility will be equipped with two state-of-the-art PSD-4 spray-drying units, allowing for future capacity expansions as demand continues to grow. Additional upgrades to the Bend site include supporting infrastructure for solvent handling and storage. The project also integrates energy-efficient utility and process systems and enhanced emission control technologies to reduce overall facility energy demand.
The new facility, expected to be completed in 2029, will be delivered through a significant capital investment and will initially create more than 80 new jobs, highlighting Lonza’s commitment to expanding its manufacturing footprint in the U.S. The expansion enhances proximity to key customers and supports more resilient, regionalized supply chains for critical therapies.

Boeing to lead eVTOL jamming and spoofing research in Spain
By Web Team 10th September 2026 3 Mins Read 
Share 
LinkedIn 
Twitter 
Facebook 
Email 
Image: AdobeStock 
Boeing Aerospace Spain is to lead a three-year research project aimed at detecting and countering satellite-navigation jamming and spoofing that threatens autonomous air taxis and other advanced air mobility aircraft.
The Validation of Airspace Integration Applications and New Technologies (VARIANT) project brings together Boeing Aerospace Spain (BAS), Boeing’s digital airspace subsidiary SkyGrid and Austrian telecom software firm Dimetor to tackle interference with global navigation satellite systems (GNSS). It will integrate Dimetor’s NAVSentry platform, which uses artificial intelligence to monitor, detect and alert against jamming and spoofing across advanced air mobility (AAM) operations.
The consortium also includes safety consultants ANZEN Engineering, AI Methods and QCentroid Labs, the Carlos III University of Madrid, ANSP ENAIRE, the Polytechnic University of Madrid and Spanish air traffic management (ATM) R&D body CRIDA as subcontractors. It is partly funded by the Community of Madrid’s technological innovation directorate.
eVTOL aircraft and cargo drones could fly low and possibly autonomously in dense urban areas, relying almost entirely on GNSS for navigation in signal-hostile environments. Without a pilot to notice a fault, precise and trustworthy positioning becomes a systemic safety requirement as more aircraft share the same low-altitude airspace.
Jamming floods the signal environment with noise, causing a loss of position that the aircraft can at least detect. Spoofing broadcasts false but plausible signals, so the aircraft keeps reporting a position that is simply wrong, which in an uncrewed eVTOL can propagate undetected through the navigation system.
Rather than deploying dedicated ground receivers, NAVSentry uses existing national telecom networks, as mobile base stations already rely on GNSS for timing and act as passive interference sensors. Aggregating data from tens of thousands of these across a country creates a real-time, wide-area interference-monitoring grid without new hardware.
Dimetor says the approach gives city-scale coverage that fixed receivers cannot, showing where interference is occurring and how it is evolving so operators can reroute traffic before an aircraft enters an affected zone. The platform has already been deployed and tested on military sites.
VARIANT will assess how the detection service applies to AAM operations – including flight planning, contingency management and surveillance – across the different phases of flight, using high-fidelity simulations and real data gathering in Madrid. Alongside interference detection, it will also address ground-based traffic surveillance, local weather monitoring and vertiport resource management.
The work supports SkyGrid’s aim of building ground-based digital ATM for autonomous operations in complex urban airspace. Boeing Aerospace Spain and SkyGrid bring aerospace integration and certification expertise, while Dimetor contributes the NAVSentry platform and its telecom-data partnerships.

Chemours, DuPont and Corteva Reach Agreement to Resolve PFAS-Related Claims in North Carolina
News provided by
The Chemours Company
Sep 10, 2026, 06:45 ET
Share this article
Share to X 
Share this article
Share to X 
Resolves litigations brought by the State of North Carolina and 11 local entities relating to PFAS and other historical discharges from Fayetteville Works, as well as the State's claims of PFAS contamination unrelated to that site, including from the use of aqueous film forming foam ("AFFF").
Overall settlement payments total $455 million over 15 years; Chemours' 50% share of payments of approximately $180 million on a net present value basis, which are covered by existing accruals.
The settlement recognizes the significant investments and progress made under the 2019 Consent Order with the State of North Carolina, including substantial reductions in PFAS emissions from Fayetteville Works and mitigation of off-site impacts in the surrounding communities.
WILMINGTON, Del. , Sept. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Chemours Company (NYSE: CC ) (the "Company") today announced that, along with DuPont de Nemours, Inc. ("Dupont") and Corteva, Inc. ("Corteva"), it has entered into a settlement (the "Settlement") with the State of North Carolina (the "State") and 11 local entities* in the vicinity of the Company's Fayetteville Works facility that were excluded from the U.S. Public Water System Class Settlement approved in 2024.
The Settlement resolves litigations brought by the State and the settling local entities relating to PFAS and other historical discharges from Fayetteville Works, as well as the State's claims of PFAS contamination unrelated to that site, including from the use of AFFF.
The settlement also acknowledges the substantial progress made under the Company's 2019 Consent Order with the State (the "Consent Order"). Since 2019, Chemours has made substantial investments to significantly reduce PFAS emissions from Fayetteville Works and mitigate off-site impacts in the surrounding communities. The agreement recognizes that several Consent Order provisions have been completed and establishes procedures to address certain remaining obligations relating to off-site areas, including implementation of drinking water programs.
Settlement payments will total $455 million (the "Settlement Amount") over a 15-year period beginning within 30 days of the execution date of the agreement. Chemours' share of expected payments over the next twelve months is approximately $50 million. Of the total settlement amount, $18 million is attributed to alleged PFAS contamination unrelated to Fayetteville Works.
The terms of the Settlement, including a further description of claims released and not released, are set forth in the Settlement Agreement, which remains subject to entry of dismissals of the covered litigations.
Consistent with the January 2021 Memorandum of Understanding ("MOU") between the Company, DuPont, and Corteva, Chemours will be responsible for 50% of settlement payments, and DuPont and Corteva will be responsible for the remaining 50%. In addition, Chemours, DuPont, and Corteva have mutually worked together to reach certain understandings concerning the MOU, including the valuation of the Settlement and potential future multi-year settlements on a net present value basis for purposes of calculating qualified spend, as they continue to work together to address legacy PFAS-related litigation matters. Pursuant to these understandings, for purposes of calculating the amount of qualified spend, the Settlement Amount will account for approximately $210 million.
In addition, all future contributions to the MOU escrow account will be considered satisfied, including Chemours' $50 million escrow contribution that would have been due in September 2026. 
This settlement marks further progress under the Strengthening the Long-Term Pillar of Chemours' Pathway to Thrive strategy and ongoing efforts to address legacy liabilities and community concerns. The agreement provides greater clarity regarding the liabilities associated with these matters, acknowledges the significant progress already made at Fayetteville Works, and supports the Company's continued operation of this important manufacturing facility.
* The 11 local entities are Bladen County, Brunswick County, Columbus County, Cumberland County, New Hanover County, Robeson County, Sampson County, Town of Wrightsville Beach, City of Lumberton, Village of Bald Head Island, and Lower Cape Fear Water and Sewer Authority.

Amkor Technology increases Arizona semiconductor campus investment to $12bn
By
Alexa Hornbeck 
| Published: 10-Sep-2026 
Design & Build 
Containment 
The semiconductor packaging and test services provider will add 60,000 sqm of cleanroom space to its Arizona campus, taking the site’s total cleanroom footprint to approximately 93,000 sqm
Amkor Technology is expanding its planned investment in a new advanced semiconductor packaging and test campus in Arizona to approximately $12bn, as customer commitments drive the addition of a second phase.
The company said demand has surpassed the 33,000 sqm of cleanroom capacity planned for Phase 1 of the campus.
Phase 2 will add a further 60,000 sqm, bringing the total cleanroom area across the site to around 93,000 sqm. 
The project is being developed as a multi-phase semiconductor manufacturing campus in Peoria, Arizona, with capabilities spanning wafer bump, probe, assembly and test.
Amkor said the expansion will increase the scale of advanced packaging manufacturing in the US, with the combined phases expected to support a workforce of more than 3,500 Arizona-based employees. 
The campus is intended to become the first US outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) production site providing advanced packaging at high volume, offering customers a domestic turnkey manufacturing platform.
Construction of Phase 2 is expected to begin in late 2027, with completion targeted for the end of 2029. The wider campus covers approximately 170 acres, allowing for further expansion in response to customer demand. 
Amkor originally broke ground on the Arizona campus in October 2025, when the planned investment stood at $7bn across two phases. The project was initially planned to provide more than 750,000 sq ft of cleanroom space. 
The latest expansion follows a series of developments around Amkor’s US advanced packaging strategy.
In June, the company announced a 10-year agreement with TSMC covering advanced packaging and testing services in Arizona, while in July it announced a multi-year partnership with NVIDIA supported by a $1.5bn advanced packaging and development agreement.
“This next phase reflects the confidence our customers have placed in Amkor, the critical role advanced packaging plays in enabling the future of semiconductor innovation, and the strategic importance of our Arizona campus," said Kevin Engel, President and CEO of Amkor Technology.
The Arizona campus will support semiconductor applications including artificial intelligence, data centres, smartphones, automotive and wearable devices.

NY Creates Announces Participation in 12-Inch Mask Industry Initiative to Advance High NA EUV Lithography Ecosystem
View the Original 12-Inch Mask Industry Initiative News Release Here. 
Albany, NY — NY Creates (the New York Center for Research, Economic Advancement, Technology, Engineering, and Science) today announced its inclusion in the 12-inch mask industry initiative, a newly formed collaboration designed to strengthen the high numerical aperture extreme ultraviolet (high NA EUV) lithography ecosystem and support the industry’s transition toward larger masks that can be used to increase the area in which chip components at the smallest, next-generation nodes can be printed.
This effort dovetails with NY Creates’ upcoming high NA EUV lithography capabilities, which are part of its High NA EUV Lithography Center. Underpinning this Center is NY Creates’ partnership ecosystem and semiconductor expertise, combined with ASML’s High NA EUV equipment that can print chip components at the sub 1nm node, leading to faster, more powerful computing capabilities. As part of this 12-inch mask effort to advance high NA EUV lithography readiness, NY Creates is participating alongside a number of industry stakeholders committed to ensuring that the technology can be successfully developed, integrated, and scaled for future high-volume manufacturing applications.
“High NA EUV lithography represents one of the most significant technological advancements in semiconductor manufacturing, and its successful adoption will depend on unprecedented collaboration across the global semiconductor ecosystem,” said Dave Anderson, President and CEO of NY Creates. “This initiative reflects the industry’s shared commitment to solving complex technical challenges through collaborative research and development, and Creates is proud to contribute its convening power, infrastructure, and ecosystem expertise to accelerate progress with ASML, TSMC, and partners.”
Today’s standard EUV masks, or reticle size, measure approximately 6-by-6-inches. High NA EUV technology uses advanced optics to deliver higher resolution, but those optics reduce the area that can be printed on a wafer in a single exposure. For larger chips, this can require multiple exposures to be stitched together, adding complexity and potentially affecting manufacturing efficiency and yield.
To address this challenge, industry leaders are exploring a larger 6-by-12-inch mask format. A larger mask could enable larger areas of a chip to be printed in a single exposure, reducing the need for stitching and improving productivity. Making this transition, however, would require advances across the broader mask ecosystem, including mask blanks, writing and inspection equipment, pellicles, handling systems, and manufacturing infrastructure.
As a neutral hub, NY Creates’ Albany NanoTech Complex provides a collaborative infrastructure to unite key stakeholders across the semiconductor industry, supporting leading-edge R&D efforts and accelerating the readiness required for high NA EUV lithography adoption. By working alongside industry leaders and research partners, NY Creates’ participation in the initiative further reinforces the organization’s commitment to facilitating industry-wide collaboration and strengthening the cutting-edge capabilities needed for next-generation advances that will shape the future of semiconductor innovation, and ultimately, the technologies we all rely on.

content_text:
AprilBio-Backed Curigin Seeks RNA Technology Collaboration with Bayer in Boston
Add preferred source 
Curigin, an RNA drug development company in which South Korea's AprilBio holds a strategic stake, will participate in the Bayer Co.Lab Showcase at RESI Boston on September 22. Curigin has been selected as one of seven promising biotech companies from South Korea and Japan to present its proprietary siRNA technology and RNA therapeutic platform to Bayer executives, with discussions planned around potential technology transfer, co-development, and other collaboration opportunities. This marks Curigin's first appearance on a global stage since AprilBio acquired a 25.26% stake for approximately 2.89 billion won (approximately $2.1 million) in July, becoming the second-largest shareholder. The two companies are jointly developing next-generation antibody-oligonucleotide conjugates (AOCs) by combining AprilBio's platform technology with Curigin's dual-targeting siRNA technology.
Key Elements 
Curigin AprilBio Bayer Bayer Co.Lab RESI Boston siRNA Antibody-Oligonucleotide Conjugate Novartis Avidity Biosciences Lundbeck Evommune Crafton Biotechnology Kanjin Therapeutics Life Science Nation 
South Korea's AprilBio-backed RNA drug development company Curigin will discuss potential technology collaboration with global pharmaceutical giant Bayer in Boston on September 22. Curigin is set to participate in RESI Boston, a global showcase hosted by Bayer Co.Lab — Bayer's innovation ecosystem — where it will present its proprietary siRNA technology and RNA-based therapeutic platform.
This Boston visit goes beyond simple event participation. Bayer selected a subset of companies it had previously met in South Korea to present their technologies directly to key decision-makers in the United States and explore follow-up collaboration opportunities. Bayer plans to send core business development & licensing (BD&L) executives to the event, drawing attention to whether Curigin's technology could lead to a technology export deal with a global big pharma company.
Curigin will be introduced as one of seven promising biotech companies from South Korea and Japan at the session titled "Connecting Asian Biotech Innovation with Global Partners: A Bayer Co.Lab Showcase." At the event, Curigin will present its capabilities as a company developing "RNA-based therapeutic technologies across multiple disease areas," showcasing its proprietary siRNA technology, RNA-based drug development capabilities, and pipeline. The company plans to explore various commercialization opportunities including technology transfer, co-development, and strategic partnerships with global pharmaceutical and biotech companies.
According to the list released by organizer Life Science Nation (LSN), the showcase will run for two hours starting at 2:00 p.m. local time on September 22, the first day of the event, featuring five South Korean companies and two Japanese companies.
Company Country Core Technology 
artiCure South Korea Tumor-selective replicating gene therapy targeting solid tumors 
Crafton Biotechnology Japan mRNA therapeutics incorporating computational approaches 
Curigin South Korea RNA-based therapeutic technologies across multiple disease areas 
Elisigen South Korea Next-generation gene therapy focused on ophthalmology 
Genome & Company South Korea Microbiome-based drug discovery and development 
ILIAS Biologics South Korea Exosome-based therapeutics for inflammatory and fibrotic diseases 
Kanjin Therapeutics Japan RNA therapeutics including siRNA and antisense 
Note: Company names and core technologies are based on the organizer's published list.
Among the Japanese participants, Crafton Biotechnology is an mRNA-focused company based at a Nagoya University incubation facility, while Kanjin Therapeutics develops RNA therapeutics using siRNA and antisense approaches. The session will effectively showcase RNA therapeutic technologies from both South Korea and Japan side by side. On Bayer's side, in addition to a senior director of strategy and portfolio at Co.Lab and BD&L executives, the head of Bayer's "Collaborate to Cure Japan Hub" — the company's Japan collaboration base — is also scheduled to attend.
AprilBio's Strategic Investment and Collaboration Framework
This event carries significant weight as it marks the first time Curigin's RNA technology is being introduced on a global stage since AprilBio made a strategic investment in the company earlier this year to expand its RNA drug development business.
The collaboration between the two companies began in January with a memorandum of understanding (MOU) for joint research on AOCs, combining AprilBio's multi-antibody platform "REMAP" with Curigin's dual-targeting siRNA technology.
In July, AprilBio invested approximately 2.89 billion won (approximately $2.1 million) to acquire a 25.26% stake in Curigin, becoming the second-largest shareholder. Along with the investment, AprilBio also secured options on Curigin's siRNA platform and priority rights for co-development. The two companies are pursuing development of next-generation antibody-oligonucleotide conjugates (AOCs) by combining AprilBio's platform technology with Curigin's dual-targeting siRNA technology.
On July 21, the day after the stake acquisition was announced, AprilBio also signed a license-in (L/I) agreement with Curigin to bring in a metabolic disease therapeutic candidate based on the dual-targeting siRNA platform. The contract amount and target molecule were not disclosed at the counterparty's request, but the deal exceeds 10% of AprilBio's most recent fiscal year revenue (2.172 billion won). The licensed molecule is designed to simultaneously suppress two different genes with a single siRNA, using GalNAc — which binds to hepatocyte surface receptors — to deliver the drug to the liver. The company explained that the molecule could be developed as a treatment for metabolic diseases such as dyslipidemia, regulating both LDL cholesterol and triglycerides. If AprilBio licenses this molecule to a third party, revenue will be shared between the two companies at a pre-agreed ratio.
Curigin has recently been expanding its technological competitiveness, including obtaining health technology certification for its siRNA-based dual-targeting therapeutic technology. Combining Curigin's dual-targeting siRNA technology with AprilBio's targeted delivery platform is expected to create new business opportunities in the RNA therapeutics space. The Bayer Co.Lab Showcase is also meaningful in that it provides an opportunity to introduce this technology combination to the global pharmaceutical and biotech industry.
AprilBio is expanding its business scope from traditional antibody-based drug development into RNA therapeutics. Through its collaboration with Curigin, the company aims to expand its RNA drug portfolio by securing AOC and siRNA candidates.
An AprilBio representative said, "We are securing new growth engines in the RNA therapeutics space by combining the siRNA technology obtained through our strategic investment in Curigin with our platform technology. Through this Bayer Co.Lab global showcase, we expect Curigin's technological competitiveness to gain broader recognition in the global pharmaceutical and biotech market, creating positive opportunities for AprilBio's RNA business expansion going forward."
The representative added, "As global pharmaceutical companies are increasingly interested in RNA therapeutics and next-generation delivery technologies, we plan to actively expand global business development and co-development opportunities based on our collaboration with Curigin."
AprilBio's Technology Deal Track Record
Prior to the Curigin investment, AprilBio had already completed two technology export deals, licensing its own drug candidates to European and U.S. pharmaceutical companies. Both candidates feature designs that extend in vivo half-life through serum albumin binding.
Timing Counterparty Subject Deal Terms 
October 2021 Lundbeck (Denmark) APB-A1 (anti-CD40L, neuroimmune diseases) technology export $16 million upfront, up to $432 million in milestones, tiered royalties 
June 2024 Evommune (U.S.) APB-R3 (IL-18 targeting, EVO301) technology export Total $475 million, including $15 million upfront 
January 2026 Curigin (South Korea) AOC joint research Memorandum of Understanding 
July 2026 Curigin (South Korea) 25.26% stake acquisition Approximately 2.89 billion won (approximately $2.1 million) 
July 2026 Curigin (South Korea) License-in of metabolic disease siRNA candidate Undisclosed (exceeds 10% of most recent fiscal year revenue) 
Note: Milestones are conditional payments made in stages based on development, regulatory, and commercial achievements; the total contract value is not fully paid out.
According to company history, APB-A1 entered Phase 1b clinical trials led by Lundbeck in October 2024, and APB-R3 entered Phase 2a clinical trials led by Evommune in November of the same year.
Global RNA Therapeutics Market and Outlook
The RNA therapeutics market has become a focal point for global pharmaceutical companies. Following the success of mRNA vaccines, various RNA-based technologies including siRNA and antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are gaining attention as next-generation therapeutic platforms. siRNA technology, in particular, can selectively suppress the expression of specific genes, offering broad applicability from rare diseases to metabolic and cardiovascular conditions.
Bayer is also expanding its investments and collaborations in next-generation therapeutic modalities, including RNA therapeutics. Bayer Co.Lab serves as a channel for discovering and commercializing innovative technologies through connections with the global biotech ecosystem. The fact that Bayer is directly selecting Asian biotech companies to meet in the United States at this showcase demonstrates the growing interest in RNA technology from the Asian region.
Bayer Co.Lab is Bayer's global life science incubator network with hubs in Cambridge, U.S.; Kobe, Japan; Shanghai, China; and Berlin, Germany. Among these, the Kobe hub is situated in the heart of one of Japan's largest biomedical innovation clusters, providing laboratory space and mentoring to early- and mid-stage startups while supporting their entry into Japanese and global markets.
The growing prominence of AOCs is also evidenced by major deals. Swiss pharmaceutical giant Novartis announced on October 26, 2025, that it would acquire U.S.-based Avidity Biosciences — which owns an AOC platform delivering drugs to muscle tissue and three late-stage clinical programs — and completed the acquisition on February 27, 2026. The deal was structured at $72 per share in cash, valued at approximately $12 billion on a fully diluted basis and approximately $11 billion in enterprise value (EV). Given that Avidity's programs are in late-stage clinical development targeting muscle diseases, there is a significant development-stage gap compared to the AOC being co-developed by AprilBio and Curigin.
If Curigin achieves co-development and research outcomes with global big pharma companies like Bayer, AprilBio — as Curigin's second-largest shareholder and the party that signed a license-in agreement with Curigin — is expected to benefit directly and indirectly. However, at the current stage, this remains an early phase of technology introduction and collaboration discussions, and whether it will lead to actual contract signing or technology export remains to be seen.
RESI Boston will be held from September 22 to 23 at the Westin Copley Place in Boston, U.S. Bayer Co.Lab is participating as the title sponsor of the event. Following the in-person event, online partnering sessions will continue on September 25 and from September 28 to 29.

content_text:
Arkema Launches Its Tenth Capital Increase Reserved for the Group’s Current and Former Employees*
Business Wire 
September 10, 2026 6 min read 
AKE.PA 
PARIS-LA DÉFENSE, September 10, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )--Regulatory News: 
Arkema (Paris:AKE) is carrying out another capital increase reserved for Arkema Group's current and former employees*, in 31 countries, including France, representing around 98% of the Group's employees. The subscription period will take place from 14 September 2026 to 28 September 2026 inclusive. 
FRAMEWORK AND RATIONALE OF THE OPERATION 
The Shareholders annual general meeting of 21 May 2026 delegated its powers to the Board of Directors for the purpose of carrying out, in one or several steps, for a maximum nominal amount not exceeding €13.5 million, and within a timeframe not exceeding 26 months, an issuance of shares reserved for the Group's current and former employees*, within the framework of article L. 225-138-1 of the French Commercial Code and of article L. 3332-18 et seq. of the French Labor Code. 
In order to reinforce the existing relationship between the Group and its employees by giving them the possibility of being more closely linked to the Group's future developments and performance and in accordance with this delegation of powers, the Board of Directors decided on 21 May 2026 to once more carry out a capital increase reserved for the Group's current and former employees* up to a maximum nominal amount of €13.5 million, and to grant all powers to the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer for the purpose of carrying it out, in particular to determine the subscription price and period. 
This capital increase is offered in France, Australia, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, China, Denmark, Egypt, Ireland, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Philippines, Poland, Romania, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States, subject to local authorizations in some of those countries. 
SECURITIES OFFERED 
On 9 September 2026, the Chief Executive Officer, through delegated authority of the Board of Directors, set the subscription price and period as follows: 
- Subscription price: € 45.06 . It is equal to 75% of the average of the opening prices of the Arkema share on the Euronext Paris S.A. market during the twenty trading days preceding this day, i.e. 75% of € 60.08 . 
- Subscription period: from 14 September 2026 to 28 September 2026 inclusive. 
The maximum number of shares that may be issued is 1.35 million, with a nominal value of €10 each, i.e. a total nominal value of €13.5 million. 
Story Continues 
SUBSCRIPTION CONDITIONS 
The beneficiaries of the reserved issuance are : 
- the employees of the Group companies that have become members of the Arkema Group's Company Savings Plan (hereinafter referred to as the "PEG A") who meet a seniority requirement of at least three months at the time of subscription; and 
- former employees* or employees on early retirement who subscribed to the PEG A before their employment activities ended, provided that they have kept assets in the PEG A and subject to applicable local law. 
Type of issuance : this issuance is carried out without preferential subscription rights. The new shares shall bear right as from their date of issue, to any dividend distributed by Arkema as from that date. 
Subscription ceiling : the beneficiaries have an individual subscription ceiling equal to the counter-value of 1,000 discounted Arkema shares. In addition, the annual payments made by each beneficiary cannot exceed one quarter of gross annual remuneration. This ceiling takes into account all of the other payments that can be made by employees within the framework of their Company and/or the Group's Savings Plans. 
Lock-up applicable to the Arkema shares : pursuant to article L. 3332-25 of the French Labor Code, the current and former employees* who have subscribed to the issuance must hold their shares directly or indirectly, for a lock-up period of five years (until 27 October 2031 included), unless one of the early exit events set forth in articles L. 3324-10 and R. 3324-22 of the French Labor Code occurs for employees and former employees* residing in France. The rules regarding the lock-up period and release that may be adjusted outside of France are set out in the local supplement prepared in each country. 
Moreover, in France, employees and former employees* may finance their subscription from the FCPE AMUNDI LABEL MONÉTAIRE ESR fund, by allocation of the sums invested in 2026 and of the assets already available as of 1 June 2026 in the PEG A, up to a total amount capped at €6,000. 
Abroad, employees who subscribe to the capital increase will be awarded one free share for 4 subscribed shares within the limit of 25 shares. These shares will be granted pursuant to the 14th resolution adopted by the Shareholders annual general meeting of 22 May 2025. The delivery of these shares will take place after the end of a vesting period, which duration is specified in the documentation applicable to each country. 
SPECIAL NOTE REGARDING THE INTERNATIONAL OFFERING 
This press release does not constitute an offer to sell or a solicitation to purchase Arkema shares. The offering of Arkema shares reserved for employees will be conducted only in countries where such an offering has been registered with the competent local authorities and/or following the approval of a prospectus by the competent local authorities or in consideration of an exemption of the requirement to prepare a prospectus or register the offering. 
More generally, the offering will only be conducted in countries where all required filing procedures and/or consultation or information obligations with respect to organizations representing employees and/or notifications have been completed and the authorizations have been obtained. This press release is not destined for, and copies thereof should not be sent to, countries in which such a prospectus has not been approved or such an exemption is not available or where all of the required filing procedures and/or consultation or information obligations with respect to organizations representing employees and/or notifications have not been completed or where the authorizations have not been obtained. 
Building on its unique set of expertise in materials science, Arkema offers a portfolio of first-class technologies to address ever-growing demand for new and more sustainable materials. With the ambition to become a world leader in Specialty Materials, the Group is structured into three complementary, resilient and highly innovative segments dedicated to Specialty Materials - Adhesive Solutions, Advanced Materials, and Coating Solutions - accounting for some 85% of Group sales in 2025, and a Primary Materials segment regrouping well-positioned large scale industrials activities. Arkema offers cutting-edge technological solutions to meet the challenges of, among other things, new energies, access to water, recycling, urbanization and mobility, and fosters a permanent dialogue with all its stakeholders. The Group reported sales of around €9.1 billion in 2025 and operates in some 55 countries with 20,700 employees worldwide.

Bye’s eFlyer 2 Electric Trainer Gets FAA Approval To Begin Flight Testing 
Share
Graham Warwick 
September 09, 2026 
Bye's eFlyer 2 prototype is powered by a Safran electric motor and MagniX battery system.
Credit: Bye Aerospace
Bye Aerospace has received a special airworthiness certificate from the FAA for its eFlyer 2 full-scale prototype, clearing the way to begin flight tests of the electric training aircraft.
The FAA awarded the first eFyer 2 its experimental ticket following a detailed inspection of the completed two-seat aircraft at Bye’s facility at Centennial Airport near Denver.
Bye completed the structural build of the nonconforming prototype in July, following several months of structural testing of the composite wing, fuselage and flight controls.
The company has also completed validation testing on the complete propulsion system, including the Safran ENGINeUS 100 electric engine and MagniX Samson battery system, using a truck-mounted testbed called the “Beast,” CEO Rod Zastrow says.
“The functional testing has been completed,” he says. “We’re just doing a few confirmatory checks with our partners to ensure all of us are satisfied we’ve addressed and mitigated all the risks, not only as independent systems, but as a combined electric propulsion system. I would say we are very close to first flight.”
Bye has been working with the FAA since 2016 to advance the framework for certification of the eFlyer 2 under existing Part 23 airworthiness regulations for light aircraft, but now plans to begin with approval under the new Part 22 rule for light-sport category aircraft.
The FAA’s revamp of rules for light sport aircraft, also known as Mosaic, now allows electric propulsion. Part 22 allows manufacturers to self-certify their aircraft using industry consensus standards to demonstrate compliance with the airworthiness regulation.
“Now that Part 22 is available to us we believe our aircraft can meet the criteria in terms of speed and weight, subject to confirmation by flight test,” Zastrow says. “Our intent is to swiftly meet the consensus standards. But we still intend, over the longer term, to take everything we learn in Part 22 and apply it to Part 23 [certification].”
Bye holds letters of intent for more than 1,000 eFlyer 2s and planned four-seat eFlyer 4s from customers that include major flight training schools. Part 22 allows light sport aircraft to be used for flight training, and Zastrow says a survey of customers indicates they are willing to take a Part 22 aircraft to meet training demand and benefit from lower costs.
Zastrow says the outer mold line of the prototype is close to conforming with the type design of the production aircraft, while the Safran motor and Garmin avionics are already certified. But the rest of the electrical system is likely to evolve as a result of flight testing.
“We’re going to learn a lot from the flight-test program, and we’re likely to take that and do a maximum conforming prototype after that,” he says.
Development of the eFlyer 2 has been paced by funding, but first flight is typically a defining moment for a company aspiring to be aircraft manufacturer, and Bye believes flying the prototype will spur financial interest, Zastrow says. “We are cautiously optimistic.”
Bye is planning a test program that will explore the full flight envelope and gather data on the electric propulsion system’s functionality and reliability. Flight testing will be supported by a charging station at Centennial supplied by Australian company Electro.Aero.
Zastrow says Bye is also modifying the Beast propulsion testbed into a mobile charging vehicle to support cross-country test flights of the eFlyer 2. The truck-mounted rig was used for propulsion testing at Pikes Peak International Raceway south of Colorado Springs.
This included the ability to articulate the rig to test low-speed, multiple-angle-of-attack scenarios to assess whether the cooling provided by the annular air intake was sufficient. “All the test data came back favorably. We have not had to redesign anything,” he says.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Fox Corp.’s $22-billion acquisition of San José-based Roku, operator of streaming services and seller of hardware devices, seemed like a straightforward deal when it was announced in June: A growing media company was looking to bolster its presence in the fast-growing streaming industry.
But, on Wednesday, the Trump administration weighed in.
Fox Corp. and Roku said that the companies received requests from the Justice Department on Tuesday for additional information in connection with its review of the merger. 
While Fox and Roku downplayed the requests, saying that they had expected the outreach, the timing of the move raised eyebrows among some analysts, who said it could signal further scrutiny of the transaction by the Justice Department.

“The president has been outspoken on the fact that he will take retaliatory action against networks that say things that he doesn’t agree with, or they do things that he doesn’t agree with,” said Rob Enderle, principal analyst at advisory services firm Enderle Group. 
The action follows President Trump’s surprise over Fox’s ouster of anchor Maria Bartiromo. She was pushed out after she had shared internal company texts with the White House, which sources told The Times may have been the breaking point.
Trump said on social media that he couldn’t believe that Bartiromo will no longer have her shows on Fox. “Her fans, of which there are many, will not be happy,” he wrote on Truth Social on Sept. 3.

Associate Atty. Gen. Stanley Woodward said the Justice Department could not comment on pending matters but said in a statement: “We can affirm that this DOJ under President Trump’s leadership will continue to prioritize affordability for all Americans across our economy.”
Fox announced in June its plans to acquire Roku for $22 billion , which would give the company access to Roku’s 100 million households that use its platform to connect to different streaming services. The deal would benefit Fox’s advertising business, as well as make it less reliant on traditional pay TV platforms.
Fox and Roku said they expect the merger to be done by the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory and shareholder approval, according to a Sept 9 filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. 
“FOX and Roku will continue to work cooperatively with the DOJ in its review of the Mergers,” Fox said in its filing.
Some legal experts said it is fairly standard for the Justice Department to make an additional request for information.
“It doesn’t mean that their review is going to be more extensive than usual,” said Ray Seilie, an entertainment attorney at law firm Kinsella Holley Iser Kump Steinsapir.

For example, the Justice Department made a second request for information when it reviewed Paramount Skydance’s deal to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, he said. The merging companies typically send information that helps the government figure out what the market impact will be of a merger, he added. 
The Justice Department ultimately approved Paramount’s planned acquisition, despite opposition from some industry stakeholders. State attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America have sued Paramount over the deal, raising antitrust concerns. Others have pointed out close ties between Trump and Larry Ellison, a financial backer of the deal, who has also donated money to a group that supports Trump. Ellison’s son, David, is chief executive of Paramount Skydance. 
Legal experts and analysts said they don’t think the combination of Fox and Roku raises antitrust issues because they are not dominant players in streaming and have businesses that complement each other. 
But one wild card is Trump. 
“You never know what Trump is going to seize on and decide he wants to do,” said Bryan Sullivan, a partner with law firm Early Sullivan Wright Gizer & McRae on whether Trump will take retaliatory action through the Justice Department in the Fox-Roku deal. “It’s chaos in the federal government and it could very well happen because of that reason, but it could also just be a blip and not a big deal.” 
Times staff writer Stephen Battaglio contributed to this report.

FDA clears Bayer’s Hyrnuo in first-line lung cancer, amping up Hernexeos rivalry
By
Donavyn Coffey 
Sep 9, 2026 4:33pm 
Bayer 
NSCLC 
tyrosine kinase inhibitor 
FDA approval 
“This approval underscores the potential of precision medicine to transform outcomes by matching the right patients to the right therapy at the right time,” said Christine Roth, executive vice president, global product strategy and commercialization at Bayer. (Bayer)
In an accelerated decision , the FDA expanded Bayer’s Hyrnuo indication, granting first-line approval for a rare tumor type in patients with non-small cell lung cancer. 
Before the expansion, Hyrnuo was available only after other NSCLC treatments failed. But the FDA’s latest go-ahead makes the tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) an initial therapy option for any patient with locally advanced or metastatic non-squamous NSCLC whose tumors test positive for HER2 tyrosine kinase domain activating mutations. 
The expanded indication was won using data from Bayer’s ongoing phase 1/2 Soho-01 trial, in which Hyrnuo demonstrated a 75% objective response rate in previously untreated patients. Six percent of patients showed a complete response, and 70% showed a partial response to the twice-daily oral medication, Bayer said Wednesday. Responses lasted more than six months for 73% of patients.
This subtype of lung cancer patients are often non-smokers and “historically have a poor prognosis,” said Soho-01 lead investigator, Xiuning Le, M.D., Ph.D., of The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, in a statement. 
“This approval underscores the potential of precision medicine to transform outcomes by matching the right patients to the right therapy at the right time,” added Christine Roth, executive vice president, global product strategy and commercialization at Bayer.
The accelerated approval means Bayer will have to continue to prove Hyrnuo’s clinical benefit through post-marketing confirmatory studies. The latest approval may hinge on the outcome of Bayer's phase 3 trial, Soho-02, which is evaluating Hyrnuo versus standard of care in treatment-naïve patients with advanced HER2-mutant NSCLC. 
Related
'Better every quarter': Bayer CEO stays course on turnaround plan as pharma sales underwhelm in Q2 
The Hyrnuo expansion follows a similar first-line approval for the drug's main competitor , Boehringer Ingelheim’s oral TKI Hernexeos, in February. Because HER2 mutations represent only 2% to 4% of the NSCLC patient population, the battle for market share between the two drugs is expected to be fierce. 
Both Bayer and Boehringer's target the same mutated tumors, although Hyrnuo is specifically designated for locally advanced or metastatic non-squamous NSCLC, while Boehringer’s label holds a small distinction for unresectable or metastatic cancer.
Hyrnuo received initial FDA approval last November , just three months after Hernexeos. In that instance, the FDA signed off on the medicine as a second-line treatment after Hyrnuo logged a 71% objective response rate in the phase 1/2 Soho-01 trial in patients who received prior systemic therapy but not one that specifically targets HER2 mutations.
Earlier this year, Hyrnuo was approved in China as a second-line treatment for unresectable, locally advanced or metastatic HER2-mutant NSCLC. The drug was also granted breakthrough therapy designation in the country to expedite its potential use as a first-line treatment, and it has also secured a first-line nod in Japan.

From Power Lines to Mine Shafts: Lidar Expands the Reach of Drone Mapping
September 9, 2026 by Miriam McNabb Leave a Comment 
Ouster partnerships with GeoCue and Flyability show how next-generation lidar is supporting applications above infrastructure and deep inside confined spaces 
Two recent partnerships from lidar developer Ouster highlight the expanding role of lidar in commercial drone operations. The applications range from surveying utility infrastructure from the air to mapping confined industrial spaces where GPS and conventional cameras may not work.
Ouster and Flyability announced this week that they are building on a five-year technology partnership centered on Flyability’s Elios 3. The collision-tolerant drone is designed for inspection and mapping inside mine shafts, wastewater tunnels, tanks, industrial vessels and other difficult or hazardous spaces.
The announcement follows a partnership unveiled last week between Ouster and GeoCue . GeoCue plans to integrate Ouster’s Rev8 OS1 Max digital lidar into its TrueView drone mapping systems for utility and infrastructure surveying.
 
Together, the two applications illustrate how improvements in lidar range, resolution and data capture could support increasingly diverse drone operations.
Mapping Where GPS and Cameras Fall Short
Flyability’s Elios 3 combines a protected, collision-tolerant airframe with Ouster’s compact OS0 lidar. Lidar data feeds the drone’s SLAM and mapping systems, supporting real-time localization, flight stability and collision avoidance.
Those capabilities become especially important inside structures where GPS is unavailable. Darkness, airborne dust and surfaces without distinctive visual features can also limit camera-based navigation.
The system allows operators to capture measurable 3D representations of assets while conducting inspections, reducing the need for workers to enter potentially hazardous areas.
“Flyability has demonstrated how digital lidar can create real operational value when it is taken into environments that conventional surveying systems cannot easily reach,” said Ouster CEO Angus Pacala. “Our collaboration brings together rugged, high-density 3D sensing and a unique aerial inspection platform, helping industrial teams understand critical assets while reducing the need for people to enter hazardous spaces.”
Flyability is now evaluating Ouster’s newer Rev8 lidar technology for future inspection workflows. Ouster says the Rev8 generation increases range and resolution while adding native color to the 3D data.
“Our collaboration with Ouster began with a shared ambition: to capture reliable 3D data in places where people should not have to go,” said Adrien Briod, CTO at Flyability. “Ouster’s lidar has become a critical part of the Elios 3 mapping platform. Bringing our teams together at INTERGEO gives us the opportunity to show surveying professionals how aerial access and high-performance lidar are already changing the way complex industrial environments are documented and understood.”
The companies will demonstrate the technology at INTERGEO 2026, taking place September 15-17 in Munich, Germany.
Taking the Same Technology to Large-Scale Mapping
The GeoCue partnership puts the latest Ouster technology into a very different operating environment.
GeoCue is expanding its TrueView product line with options using Ouster’s 256-channel Rev8 OS1 Max lidar. The companies are targeting utility and infrastructure applications, including power line mapping and long-corridor surveys.
Ouster says the sensor can detect targets with 10% reflectivity at distances up to 200 meters. A smaller spot size and tighter beam are designed to help resolve thin features such as power lines and structural edges. The system also provides native color lidar data, combining color and 3D information at the sensor level.
GeoCue selected the sensor after joint flight testing and firmware tuning in Huntsville, Alabama.
“We are moving America’s drone surveying onto American sensing by pairing our TrueView payloads with Ouster’s Rev8 OS1 Max,” said Frank Darmayan, CEO of GeoCue. “This transition allows us to offer our customers a compliant, high-performance solution that delivers the survey-grade data they depend on for critical infrastructure monitoring and large-scale mapping projects.”
The Rev8 OS1 Max is also compliant with Build America, Buy America Act requirements, an important consideration for some federally funded infrastructure projects.
Lidar Expands Across Drone Applications
The two partnerships demonstrate very different uses of the same underlying sensing technology.
With GeoCue, lidar is designed to capture precise data across large infrastructure assets from above. With Flyability, lidar helps a drone navigate and map spaces that may be inaccessible from outside and unsafe for people to enter.
In both cases, the value extends beyond creating a point cloud. Lidar increasingly supports navigation, localization and autonomous operation while also generating the 3D data required for inspection and mapping.
As sensors gain range, resolution and richer data, that overlap between perception and data collection could become increasingly important. The drone is no longer simply carrying a mapping sensor. In applications such as the Elios 3, the sensor that creates the map can also help the aircraft understand where it is and operate where other navigation technologies fall short.

Nexeon raises £100 million to expand its UK silicon anode operations
Posted September 9, 2026 by Chris Ruoff & filed under Newswire , The Tech . 
Oxfordshire-based silicon anode developer Nexeon has closed a £100-million ($133-million) investment round, completed by a £52.6-million ($70-million) commitment from the UK’s National Wealth Fund . The Korea Development Bank and Honda Xcelerator Ventures, Honda’s open innovation investment program, also came in as new investors. The round follows the $170 million Nexeon raised in 2022 in a round that included Ingevity.
The National Wealth Fund’s financing will go toward a UK-based pilot manufacturing facility, R&D work and an expansion of Nexeon’s advanced manufacturing technology unit. A pilot line is where a materials supplier proves out a process at intermediate scale and makes the qualification samples cell manufacturers test before anyone commits to full production volumes.
Silicon holds far more lithium per gram than the graphite it replaces in a conventional lithium-ion anode, but it expands as it takes up that lithium, and containing the expansion over hundreds of cycles is the central engineering problem for silicon anode materials . Nexeon says its materials raise cell energy density, cut charging times and extend EV driving range.
Nexeon already makes silicon-carbon materials at a volume production plant in Gunsan, South Korea. The company has said it picked the site for pipeline supply of monosilane gas, a key precursor for the material, and for its proximity to Asian cell producers. The plant is designed so that additional reactors can be installed to scale output, according to the company.
“This investment is a strong endorsement of Nexeon’s technology and our role in enabling the next generation of lithium-ion batteries. The National Wealth Fund’s support reflects the strategic importance of our work, not only in advancing battery performance but also in strengthening the UK’s position in the global battery supply chain,” said Scott Brown, CEO of Nexeon.

Boeing, Anduril midrange interceptor advances in U.S. Army competition
Team to further develop offering to defend against cruise missiles and hostile drones.
September 09, 2026
in
Technology ,
Defense 
Boeing’s Integrated Fires Protection Capability (IFPC) Increment 2 Second Interceptor flies to intercept a target. 
The U.S. Army selected Boeing to advance to the next phase of competition for the Integrated Fires Protection Capability (IFPC) Increment 2 Second Interceptor — a capability that will be designed to protect fixed and forward operating bases from cruise missiles, militarized unmanned aerial systems (UAS) and related aerial threats.
\r\n Why it matters: This down-select provides Boeing the resources to deliver an affordable, high-performance midrange interceptor that fills the gap between other short- and long-range defenses and allows for more interceptors in each magazine for base defense.
\r\n Driving the news: The U.S. Army’s decision begins Phase 2 of its IFPC Increment 2 Second Interceptor competition, with a detailed design, system development, integration, demonstration and a competitive capability demonstration to validate performance against Army requirements.
\r\n How it works: Boeing’s interceptor combines seeker technology, a compact form factor, a solid rocket motor supplied by Anduril Rocket Motor Systems and a Modular Open Systems Architecture (MOSA).
\r\n \r\n MOSA enables faster, lower-cost upgrades by allowing seeker, avionics or software blocks to be swapped without redesigning the entire weapon.
\r\n The design targets an effective engagement radius to defend against midrange threats.
\r\n \r\n Zoom in: Last December, Boeing partnered with Anduril for their innovative solid rocket motor capacity and to build an agile industry team capable of producing at scale for the IFPC Increment 2 Second Interceptor competition.
\r\n The big picture: Boeing’s solution emphasizes affordability, magazine depth, and speed-to-target to help address cruise missile and UAS threats emerging in recent conflicts.
\r\n What they’re saying: 
\r\n \r\n Bob Ciesla, vice president of Boeing Precision Engagement Systems: “Our scalable production approach is designed to provide a reliable, affordable layer of defense against a range of aerial threats to protect the warfighter with practical, dependable capability when it matters most.”
\r\n Jim Bryan, executive director of Boeing Integrated Air and Missile Defense: “We welcome the opportunity to continue in this competition. By combining proven seeker expertise with a purpose-built interceptor, we are delivering thoughtful, effective advances in air and missile defense that meet mission needs.”
\r\n \r\n Go deeper: Read more about Boeing and Anduril’s strategic partnership here .
\r\n By Chris Bishop and Brett Anker

More than 15 companies implicated in commercial antibody image manipulation scandal 
A recent scientific report found almost 19,000 doctored images of antibodies available in the commercial market.
Millie Hoe , Reporter, BioProcess International September 9, 2026
schedule 4 Min Read 
Wikimedia, Masur 
link 
A landmark investigation published by Northwestern University’s Reese Richardson found widespread image manipulation in the commercial antibody market. In the online article, more than 15 well-known biotechnology companies were implicated in using doctored images in their antibody catalogs. 
Richardson and his colleagues found almost 19,000 images online of antibody assays that had been subject to photo editing. This included several established vendors of commercial antibodies, such as Millipore Sigma, GeneTex, and Abnova, among others. 
“As part of our ongoing quality efforts, we continue to conduct a portfolio-wide review of antibody imagery to ensure that supporting information meets our standards for accuracy and reliability,” a spokesperson for MilliporeSigma told BPI/BioXconomy. 
“When questions arise about an image, our immediate response is to remove the image and review both the image and associated product.” 
Related: “Don’t call it continuous!” AstraZeneca expert talks integrated bioprocessing at BPI 
One of the biggest companies implicated was Thermo Fisher Scientific, whose website Richardson said featured more than 5,000 doctored images affecting more than 4,000 antibody products. 
“The investigation into Thermo Fisher yielded several hundred images that showed the same background pattern as one another,” Richardson told us . “Several other vendors all sold products with the same background, which was the first indication that this was a broader industry-wide problem.” 
The compiled images also revealed a high likelihood of widespread private labeling in the commercial antibody market, where large brands sell third-party products under their own name. Several images containing validation assays such as Western blot and immunofluorescence appeared to be replicated and doctored across multiple different antibody products. 
“Many of the affected images were apparently made up wholesale,” noted Richardson. “I remain doubtful that many of these antibodies were validated, meaning that no quality control was actually performed.” 
Some of the antibody products with doctored images failed to meet the mark in validation tests in open science communities, such as Only Good Antibodies . Of the more than 50 antibody products with manipulated photos investigated, 83% failed in at least one of its listed applications. 
Andrew Lane, an immunologist and independent life sciences consultant, was not involved in the investigation but has written publicly about the revelations. He spoke with us about the findings and detailed their greater ramifications. 
“Some of the doctoring reported could be complete fabrication of results, which brings into question whether or not a particular antibody has even been tested in a specific technique,” Lane said . “If that truly is the case, then clearly customers are being misled and suppliers are making unsubstantiated claims.” 
Related: BPI Asia Digital Series 
In response to Richardson’s report, which was picked up by several major scientific journals, Thermo Fisher publicly stated that the company “takes antibody validation, specificity, and accurate product documentation seriously,” and that “the company fully stands by the data and underlying science.” 
“We are reviewing Western blot images (including those provided by third parties) on our website to ensure that any Western blot images are clearly identified as either ‘raw-unedited’ or as an image that ‘may have been edited, optimized, or otherwise adjusted,’” said Thermo Fisher. 
As well as commercial implications for the antibody market at large, Richardson pointed out that false validation assays have serious consequences within scientific research. 
“Often, scientists do not have the time or funds to properly validate their antibodies; they'll take the manufacturers at their word that the antibodies work as intended,” he said. “If the antibodies are non-sensitive or non-specific and this is not caught, this can (and often does) lead to erroneous conclusions propagating through the scientific literature.” 
Related: BPI Spring Digital Week 
Of the 15 companies implicated, six have made public statements vowing to evaluate all affected products mentioned in the report. However, until then, Richardson said it will be difficult for scientists to ensure that the antibody they pay for will meet the mark. 
“Thirty-eight percent [of antibody products with doctored images] fail every application for which data is available,” Richardson said. “I believe that the quality control and marketing of research antibodies should, at a minimum, be regulated by a public authority.” 
Lane believes the onus falls on major suppliers to be forthcoming about their quality control protocols and the production origins of their products. 
“I think companies need to be transparent not only about the images that they publish, but also about the provenance of the antibody itself,” he added. “Companies should make it clear if they are the original manufacturer of an antibody, or if a third party has manufactured the antibody.” 
“Perhaps even less than perfect results should be shown. I’m sure that companies who do undertake their own manufacturing and validation will make it even clearer after this episode.”

content_text:
Solvay confirms OneIM talks over strategic European rare-earths business
by EUToday Correspondents 
September 9, 2026 
written by EUToday Correspondents 
September 9, 2026 
Solvay confirms OneIM talks over strategic European rare-earths business
2K The Belgian chemicals group said in regulated information on 8 September that talks were continuing and that it would provide further information when appropriate. The announcement followed a Reuters report that discussions had been under way since March. OneIM did not immediately comment.
The asset at the centre of the talks is Solvay’s separation operation at La Rochelle in France. The site processes rare-earth materials used in magnets and other advanced manufacturing. Solvay describes the business as part of its broader Special Chem portfolio, which also includes fluorine products; figures for the combined portfolio should not be treated as rare-earth revenue alone.
The potential partnership comes as European governments seek alternatives to Chinese processing. Separation capacity is more difficult to build than a mine because it requires specialised chemistry, waste controls, qualified staff and long-term feedstock contracts. A change in ownership or financing could therefore affect Europe’s industrial plans even if Solvay continues to operate the plant.
Financing a supply chain
Solvay has signed a letter of intent with Brazil’s Viridis Mining and Minerals to source rare-earth feedstock for La Rochelle from the Colossus project. The arrangement is targeted for 2028 and remains subject to a definitive agreement and project development. It covers neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, terbium and other materials that can feed magnet production.
Viridis said OneIM would invest up to $75 million and become a cornerstone investor in its Brazilian project. That is financing for the upstream development, not proof that European separation capacity has already expanded. Solvay has also discussed a €15–20 million La Rochelle expansion, with heavy rare-earth separation targeted for autumn 2026.
The possible OneIM partnership could provide capital or a different ownership structure for those plans. Solvay has not disclosed a valuation, timetable or the form of any investment. Its statement makes clear that talks may end without an agreement.
EU Today has previously covered Brussels’ plans to build a critical-minerals stockpile. The Solvay discussions show the industrial side of that policy: stockpiles can provide insurance, but processing plants require steady feedstock, financing and customers over many years.
The next formal development will be a company announcement if the parties reach binding terms. Until then, La Rochelle’s capacity, the Viridis timetable and the 2028 supply target remain separate pieces of a proposed chain. Solvay’s notice gives no valuation or closing date, so the talks cannot be treated as a completed sale.

Bayer and Neste close commercial agreement to jointly scale newgold® winter canola for biofuels production
2026-0145
Bayer and Neste close commercial agreement to jointly scale newgold® winter canola for biofuels production.
