National Wealth Fund backs Nexeon’s sodium battery tech with £53 million 
The money brings the Oxfordshire-based company’s latest investment round to £100 million (US$133 million), with additional investments from the Korea Development Bank and Honda Xcelerator Ventures.
Will Norman , Senior Reporter , Informa September 2, 2026
schedule 2 Min Read 
Nexeon claims that its technology enables faster charging and higher energy density in battery systems, with a variety of applications including electric vehicles. Image: Nexeon 
The UK National Wealth Fund has invested £52.6 million (US$70 million) into silicon anode battery technology startup Nexeon. 
The money brings the Oxfordshire-based company’s latest investment round to £100 million (US$133 million), with additional investments from the Korea Development Bank and Honda Xcelerator Ventures. 
The National Wealth Fund said the investment supports Nexeon’s “continued scale-up and commercialisation activities”. The funds will go towards Nexeon’s plans for a pilot UK manufacturing facility and its ongoing research and development (R&D) efforts. 
Nexeon is developing silicon anode technology for energy storage systems, which it said can enable the production of higher energy density lithium-ion batteries. The company operates a mass production facility in South Korea and has a research base in Japan, as well as its Oxfordshire headquarters. 
Nexeon claims that its technology enables faster charging and higher energy density in battery systems, with a variety of applications including electric vehicles (EVs). 
Related: Foresight invests in 40GWh LDES cap-and-floor winning pumped hydro project in Scotland 
"Companies like Nexeon show the strength of British innovation,” said chancellor of the exchequer John Healey. “And if we are serious about growth, we must be serious about backing British businesses like this with conditions for them to start, scale and succeed here in the UK, as the National Wealth Fund are doing here.” 
Oliver Holbourn, chief executive officer of the National Wealth Fund, added: “Our investment in Nexeon is fully aligned with our mission to support clean energy innovation and economic growth. Backing advanced battery technology is key to building a globally competitive EV supply chain in the UK”. 
Scott Brown, chief executive of Nexeon, said the investment was a “strong endorsement of Nexeon’s technology and our role in enabling the next generation of lithium-ion batteries”. 
Back in January, the National Wealth Fund revealed plans to facilitate £100 million of investment into UK clean energy , prioritising battery manufacturing and energy storage alongside grid upgrades and carbon capture projects. 
Industries minister Blair McDougall said: "Hot on the heels of a £130 million investment into net zero vehicle technologies, our Modern Industrial Strategy is doubling down on frontier industries like batteries to help businesses like Nexeon grow their business, create skilled jobs and drive good growth right across the UK.” 
There have also been some efforts to onshore solar supply and manufacturing in the UK. Great British Energy invested in Naked Energy , a solar thermal company, last month.

WorkBoat Staff 
News 
Technology 
Business 
SHARE 
From left: Peter Morsbach, Hoglund CEO; Saara Kuusisto, global business line manager, marine systems, ABB’s Marine & Ports division; and Rune Braastad, president, ABB’s Marine & Ports division. Hoglund photo. 
ABB has completed its acquisition of Norwegian marine automation specialist Hoglund AS, the companies announced.
ABB has completed its acquisition of Norwegian marine automation specialist Hoglund AS, the companies announced Wednesday.
The transaction closed Sept. 1, roughly two months after the two sides announced the agreement on June 26. ABB said at the time that the deal was expected to close in the third quarter of 2026, subject to customary regulatory approvals. Financial terms were not disclosed.
The purchase covers Hoglund's global operations and its 85 employees in Norway, Poland, Romania and China. Hoglund, which is headquartered in Tonsberg, will be folded into ABB's Marine & Ports division. The company was previously owned by Eitzen Group .
At the center of the deal is Hoglund's Integrated Automation System, a modular and scalable platform now installed aboard more than 600 ships. The system pulls together data from engines, generators, and cargo systems to support safety, energy efficiency, and operational performance.
The IAS is built on ABB's own control system hardware, specifically ABB's 800M and S800 platforms, according to the companies' June announcement.
"By adding Hoglund's automation platform as a solution to ABB's product portfolio, we combine advanced marine automation capabilities with global reach and an extensive service network, creating a powerful competitive advantage," said Rune Braastad, president of ABB's Marine & Ports division. "This gives us the opportunity to grow our automation portfolio, address a wider range of vessel types, and serve their evolving needs even better than before. I'm delighted to welcome our new colleagues from Hoglund. Together, we will drive innovation and create lasting value for shipowners, operators, and yards."
"For me, today marks a recognition of the automation technology, expertise, and experience we have built at Hoglund over the past 30 years," said Hoglund CEO Peter Morsbach. "As we take our next steps together as part of ABB, I am excited to build on the strengths of Hoglund and ABB together, advancing marine automation for the benefit of customers worldwide."
Saara Kuusisto, global business line manager for marine systems in ABB's Marine & Ports division, said the combined operation would broaden what the company can offer shipowners.
"Together, we will strengthen our automation expertise and expand our capabilities to deliver even more comprehensive integrated solutions to ships worldwide," Kuusisto said. "We will build on Hoglund's distinctive values while continuing to focus on what matters most to our customers."

Nexeon raises £100m as National Wealth Fund invests
Abingdon firm is developing silicon anode materials which will help to reduce charging times and extend range of electric vehicles
Share: 
Listen to article 
EnviroTech Investment Manufacturing Battery startup Nexeon has secured backing from the National Wealth Fund as part of a £100 million funding round. 
The National Wealth Fund has committed £52.6m, with other new investors in the round including the Korea Development Bank and Honda Xcelerator Ventures. 
Nexeon, headquartered in Abingdon near Oxford, is developing silicon anode materials which enable production of higher energy density lithium-ion batteries, helping to reduce charging times and extend the range of electric vehicles. 
The investment round supports the company’s continued scale-up and commercialisation activities and marks another key milestone in the pathway to high-volume manufacturing and global customer adoption. 
The National Wealth Fund’s financing will support Nexeon’s development of a UK-based pilot manufacturing facility, directly supporting their research and development activities and allowing the expansion of its advanced manufacturing technology unit, creating a number of new highly skilled jobs. 
By investing in innovative battery technologies and expanding local manufacturing capacity, the Fund says its investment will help to decarbonise supply chains, boost place-based investment and strengthen sovereign capabilities — supporting all three of the National Wealth Fund’s strategic ambitions. 
Honda Xcelerator Ventures is the global open innovation program of the Honda Motor Co. Ltd., and invests in technologies shaping the future of mobility and electrification. The Korea Development Bank is a leading policy bank in South Korea, focused on supporting industrial innovation and global expansion of Korean-linked manufacturing ecosystems. 
£100m competition backs British AI firms to fix public services 
Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey MP said: “Companies like Nexeon show the strength of British innovation. And if we are serious about growth, we must be serious about backing British businesses like this with conditions for them to start, scale and succeed here in the UK, as the National Wealth Fund are doing here. That’s how we’ll get good growth and jobs in every postcode.” 
Oliver Holbourn, CEO of the National Wealth Fund, said: “Our investment in Nexeon is fully aligned with our mission to support clean energy innovation and economic growth. Backing advanced battery technology is key to building a globally competitive EV supply chain in the UK, as the thought-leadership paper we recently published identifies. 
“This investment will help unlock private capital, support high-value jobs and drive regional growth, while helping to position the UK at the forefront of innovation in the battery sector.” 
Dr Scott Brown (pictured), CEO of Nexeon, said: “This investment is a strong endorsement of Nexeon’s technology and our role in enabling the next generation of lithium-ion batteries. The National Wealth Fund’s support reflects the strategic importance of our work, not only in advancing battery performance but also in strengthening the UK’s position in the global battery supply chain.” 
David Lamb, CFO at Nexeon, added: “We continue to strengthen our shareholder register with the addition of the Korea Development Bank, Honda and the National Wealth Fund. The quality of the Nexeon commercial proposition is reflected in the quality of investors we continue to attract.”

Axelspace Announces Partnership with Airbus Defence and Space to Deliver Satellite Imagery to a Broader Market 
SEP - 02 - 2026
PRESS
Axelspace Corporation (“Axelspace”), a leading microsatellite company committed to making “Space within Your Reach,” announced today a new agreement with Airbus Defence and Space, a global leader in Earth observation including optical and radar satellite imagery, to provide mid-resolution optical images captured by Axelspace’s Earth observation microsatellites “GRUS.” Under this strategic partnership, we will develop and deliver innovative solutions that meet long-term customer needs for utilizing satellite imagery.
GRUS is Axelspace’s series of approximately 100 kg-class optical Earth observation satellites. GRUS-1 is currently operated as a four-satellite constellation, delivering high-frequency, wide-area imagery. This imagery, together with value-added solutions derived through processing and analysis, supports a broad range of industries, including agriculture, land management, environmental monitoring, and finance. On July 7, 2026, Axelspace launched seven next-generation GRUS-3 satellites. Following their initial operations, they will be integrated into the GRUS constellation, expanding it to more than 10 satellites.
Through this partnership, Axelspace — which operates the Earth observation microsatellites “GRUS” — will combine its technology with Airbus’s extensive industry expertise and strong customer relationships. Together, the two companies will provide tailored solutions to meet the needs of customers across a wide range of industries.
Yuya Nakamura, President and CEO of Axelspace Corporation, and Kévin Boverie, Head of Portfolio, Geospatial Solutions, Space Digital, Airbus Defence and Space 
Eric Even, Senior Vice President, Airbus Defence and Space, commented; 
“Partnering with Axelspace creates a strong bridge for space technology and expertise between Japan and Europe. By integrating Axelspace’s agile monitoring capabilities with Airbus’s industry-leading very high-quality imagery, we are expanding our global coverage and revisit capabilities to meet our customers’ operational needs.”
Yuya Nakamura, President and CEO, Axelspace Corporation, commented; 
“We are delighted to establish this partnership with Airbus Defence and Space, a global leader in the space and defense industry with a strong presence across Europe and around the world. By providing our medium-resolution optical satellite imagery, captured with broad coverage and high revisit frequency, we believe this collaboration will further enhance the breadth, quality, and volume of satellite data available to customers, enabling a wider range of industries to benefit from Earth observation insights. Through this partnership, we look forward to working closely with Airbus Defence and Space to accelerate the adoption of Earth observation data across Europe, combining their deep industry expertise and strong customer relationships with Axelspace’s satellite technology.”
About Axelspace
Guided by its vision—“Space within Your Reach”—Axelspace has been at the forefront of microsatellite innovation since its founding in 2008. Leveraging cutting-edge expertise in microsatellite design, manufacturing, and on-orbit operations, the company is redefining how people and industries access space. Its flagship businesses, AxelLiner, which provides satellite development and operation services to help customers realize their space missions, and AxelGlobe, which delivers Earth observation data through Axelspace’s proprietary optical satellite constellation, are driving a new era of space utilization. Through these initiatives, Axelspace is shaping a future where space is accessible and within reach for everyone.

A battery materials company has achieved a major quality certification at its first commercial-scale production plant.
Nexeon, based in Oxfordshire, UK, has announced that its facility in Gunsan, South Korea, has been awarded ISO 9001:2015 certification.
The plant produces advanced silicon-carbon anode materials for lithium-ion batteries and was declared production-ready in December 2025.
Dr Scott Brown, CEO of Nexeon, said: "Achieving ISO 9001 certification at Gunsan is an important step as we move from commissioning our first commercial production facility to supplying customers at scale.

"Quality and consistency are fundamental to our ability to support the world’s leading battery and automotive companies, and this certification demonstrates the strength of the systems we have put in place to achieve that."
ISO 9001 certification is an internationally recognised standard for quality management systems and demonstrates that the Gunsan facility meets rigorous requirements in manufacturing, process management, and continuous improvement.
Nexeon said it provides customers with confidence in the company’s ability to deliver consistent product quality as production scales.
The Gunsan site is strategically located with direct access to monosilane - a key material in silicon-carbon anodes - and close to major battery manufacturers in Asia.
The facility has been designed to allow for capacity expansion by adding additional reactors to meet growing customer demand.
Nexeon continues to progress customer qualification programmes under automotive quality standards.

Hatchet Lake Denesuline First Nation reaches treaty land settlement
by MBC News | Sep 1, 2026 
Hatchet Lake Denesuline First Nation has reached a Treaty Land Entitlement settlement with the federal and Saskatchewan governments. 
Chief Bartholomew J. Tsannie, federal Secretary of State for Rural Development Buckley Belanger, and Saskatchewan Minister Responsible for First Nations, Métis and Northern Affairs Eric Schmalz announced the agreement today. 
“This settlement has been a long time coming for the people of Hatchet Lake Denesuline First Nation. Our ancestors entered into Treaty 10 with the understanding that its promises would be honoured, including the land that was owed to our people. Today, we honour the generations who carried this claim forward and whose determination brought us here. This agreement gives our Nation an opportunity to invest in our community and create a stronger future for our children and grandchildren,” said Chief Bartholomew J. Tsannie, Hatchet Lake Denesuline First Nation.
The settlement addresses a claim that Hatchet Lake Denesuline First Nation did not receive all of the reserve land promised under Treaty 10, signed in 1907. 
“Treaties are promises, and for too long, the promises made to Hatchet Lake Denesuline First Nation under Treaty 10 were not fully honoured. This settlement cannot undo that history, but it recognizes the wrong that was done and takes a meaningful step toward righting it. I’m proud that Canada is fulfilling its responsibility and helping create new opportunities for Hatchet Lake to invest in its land, its community, and its future,” explained Buckley Belanger, Secretary of State (Rural Development).
Under the agreement, the First Nation will receive $29,602,664 in compensation and may apply to add up to 28,118 acres to its reserve lands through the federal Additions to Reserve process. 
“Reaching this settlement together, we help support Hatchet Lake Denesuline First Nation in a meaningful way with new opportunities for community development, investment and long-term growth. Saskatchewan continues working with First Nations and the Government of Canada to strengthen relationships and support a stronger future for Indigenous communities across our province, while honouring outstanding obligations,” said Eric Schmalz, Minister Responsible for First Nations, Métis and Northern Affairs.
Officials say the settlement supports reconciliation and will provide opportunities for community development, infrastructure investment, and economic growth. 
In 1992, 25 First Nations, along with the federal and Saskatchewan governments, signed the Saskatchewan Treaty Land Entitlement Framework Agreement to resolve outstanding treaty land entitlement obligations. 
Since then, an additional 12 treaty land entitlement agreements have been reached with individual First Nations. 
(TOP PHOTO – Hatchet Lake community members pose for a photo following the announcement. Photo provided)

Moderna's Cancer Vaccine Nears Commercialization…South Korean Oncologist Flags 'Real-World Hurdles'
Add preferred source 
Moderna and Merck's jointly developed personalized mRNA cancer vaccine has succeeded in a Phase 3 melanoma trial, opening a new chapter in cancer treatment. Dr. Dae Ho Lee, a professor at Asan Medical Center in Seoul, explained that unlike conventional cancer drugs, this therapy analyzes each patient's tumor to design a bespoke treatment. However, significant real-world barriers remain: custom manufacturing takes three to six weeks, and the cost and infrastructure burden are substantial. AI plays a pivotal role in antigen selection, an area that constitutes each company's proprietary trade secrets. Melanoma commercialization is projected for 2027, but South Korea faces hurdles including the absence of manufacturing and logistics systems and health insurance reimbursement issues. Phase 3 results for lung cancer are expected as early as next year.
Key Elements 
Moderna Merck Dae Ho Lee Asan Medical Center mRNA cancer vaccine Keytruda Intismeran Autogene Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer melanoma 
As the personalized messenger RNA (mRNA) cancer vaccine posts positive Phase 3 results in melanoma and is hailed as opening a new era in cancer treatment, clinical practitioners are pointing to cost, infrastructure, and time as the next set of real-world challenges—separate from the technology's promise.
Dr. Dae Ho Lee, a professor of medical oncology at Asan Medical Center in Seoul, is participating in the lung cancer clinical trial of "Intismeran Autogene," the personalized mRNA cancer vaccine co-developed by Moderna and Merck. In an interview with Hankyung Business, he explained that this therapeutic strategy starts from a fundamentally different premise than conventional cancer drugs.
Existing targeted therapies and immunotherapies work by selecting from a menu of already-manufactured drugs to find one that suits the patient. An mRNA cancer vaccine, by contrast, compares the patient's tumor tissue with normal tissue to identify neoantigens that appear only on cancer cells, then designs a treatment exclusively for that patient. Dr. Lee likened the difference to "off-the-rack clothing versus a bespoke suit."
The potential has been confirmed, but the mountain ahead is formidable. Custom manufacturing requires the entire pipeline for each patient: tumor analysis, antigen selection, mRNA design, manufacturing, and transport. The process currently takes roughly three to six weeks—a substantial wait for stage 4 patients who need treatment urgently.
"Having the technology alone isn't enough," he stressed. "Connecting the entire chain—from analysis to manufacturing to logistics—costs money." In practice, the most viable approach is to begin standard treatment first while the personalized vaccine is being manufactured, then administer it as an add-on once ready.
Antigen Selection Is the Make-or-Break…AI Holds the Key
The most challenging part is identifying the "truly good antigens." Cancer cells generate millions of protein data points, and it is nearly impossible to determine in advance which antigens will actually deliver therapeutic efficacy. Even when computational analysis narrows the field to roughly 100 candidates, there is no way to know how many are genuine winners.
Artificial intelligence is the core enabler of this massive analytical undertaking. Normal and tumor tissue must be precisely compared, and researchers must verify from multiple angles whether the relevant RNA actually expresses well as protein. "Which antigens are ultimately selected and baked into the vaccine is the crux—and that depends entirely on each biotech company's AI algorithms and analytical know-how," Dr. Lee said. This is a company's core trade secret and remains undisclosed.
Commercialization Outlook and South Korea's Reality
On the prospect that melanoma commercialization could begin in 2027, Dr. Lee responded, "I think it's possible." Approvals are likely to come first in the United States, Europe, and China—countries that participated in the clinical trials.
However, regulatory approval and actual clinical use are separate matters. Personalized therapy is not something that can simply be imported and used like a conventional pharmaceutical. A patient's tumor must be sent for analysis, a treatment tailored to that patient must be manufactured, and then it must be shipped back and administered. This requires a dedicated system linking manufacturing and logistics.
"South Korea currently lacks such a system," Dr. Lee pointed out. If treatment costs are prohibitively high and patient volumes are low, companies have little incentive to build separate manufacturing and logistics infrastructure in South Korea. Integration with South Korea's national health insurance reimbursement framework is another critical variable.
Lessons from mRNA Technology and the Challenge for South Korean Biotech
He diagnosed that South Korea's biotech industry has developed around generics over the past 15 to 20 years, leaving innovation underfunded. COVID-19, in particular, was a crucial opportunity to develop mRNA technology firsthand, yet South Korea ultimately failed to produce its own COVID-19 mRNA vaccine.
Cancer mRNA vaccines are far more complex than COVID-19 vaccines. A COVID-19 vaccine targets a single antigen, whereas cancer differs from patient to patient and requires identifying multiple antigens. "Being able to make mRNA doesn't mean you can develop the entire platform," Dr. Lee said. "We need to identify which parts of the overall platform we can be competitive in." He emphasized that just as South Korea has found competitive niches in semiconductors and data centers rather than building AI from scratch, the biotech sector also requires focus and strategic prioritization.
Lung Cancer Trial Results Expected Next Year
For the ongoing Phase 3 non-small cell lung cancer trial involving approximately 900 patients worldwide, Asan Medical Center has already completed enrollment of South Korean patients. Results from this study are expected as early as next year. Separately, another lung cancer trial including stage 4 patients is also underway.
Dr. Lee's outlook is that the next decade will be less about which therapy to use alone and more about finding the optimal combinations of multiple treatments. The combination of CAR-T—which "manufactures soldiers"—mRNA vaccines—which "identify attack targets"—and Keytruda (pembrolizumab)—which "strengthens the soldiers"—could emerge as a key research priority.
On the melanoma trial success, he said, "The significance is that it confirms the personalized mRNA cancer vaccine strategy itself is viable," while adding, "This study is a beginning, not an end." The results confirmed in melanoma must now be validated in other cancer types including lung cancer, and separately in early-stage patients versus advanced and stage 4 patients.

Elliott Tries to Put Air Liquide Under Pressure
Mark Nichols 
September 1, 2026 5 min read 
AI.PA 
NVDA 
AIQUY 
Elliott Tries to Put Air Liquide Under Pressure - Moby THE GIST 
Our analysts just identified a stock with the potential to be the next Nvidia. Tell us how you invest and we'll show you why it's our #1 pick. Tap here. 
French gases group Air Liquide is getting the activist-investor treatment. 
Elliott reportedly built a stake and wants the firm to sharpen margins. Investors liked the idea, sending the shares higher as the market started pricing in a little less patience and a little more pressure. 
WHAT HAPPENED 
Elliott's been engaging with the company for months, though the the size of the stake is not known. The message, however, is clear: improve margins and compete harder with the sector's best operators. 
Air Liquide is not exactly a wounded minnow. The Paris-based group is worth about €108 billion (about $125 billion) and supplies gases including oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen to factories, hospitals, semiconductor plants and energy customers. It is one of Europe's major industrial champions. But activists don't usually arrive because everything looks perfect. 
Shares in Air Liquide rose as much as 4.2% on Tuesday and were up around 3% by late morning in London, putting the stock on track for its biggest one-day gain in six months. The shares have gained roughly 20% this year. 
The central issue is profitability. Linde's operating margin stood at about 30% in mid-2026, compared with roughly 21% for Air Liquide. That nine-point gap has become the activist bullseye. 
The gap is not new, but it has become harder to ignore. Linde's operational optimization has delivered stronger profitability, while Air Liquide's lower sales per employee suggest there may still be room to improve efficiency. 
The timing also matters. Air Liquide is due to hold a capital markets day in October, and investors are already watching for a more aggressive margin roadmap, efficiency targets or a share buyback. A buyback announcement could become a near-term catalyst for the stock. 
Air Liquide also has big growth levers. Its investment backlog stands at a record €5.5 billion, supporting around 75 major global industrial projects. Those projects are concentrated in higher-growth areas including AI-linked semiconductors, electronics and the energy transition. 
Recent spending includes more than $170 million to support SK Hynix in Indiana, $160 million for a semiconductor gas facility in Arizona, $150 million for a fab expansion in Idaho and more than €250 million to anchor a European semiconductor hub in Dresden. The company also opened a large-scale plant for advanced deposition and etching materials in Taiwan earlier this year. 
Story Continues 
That gives Elliott a slightly different story from the usual activist playbook. This is not just "cut costs and send cash back." It is "prove the growth is translating into enough profit." 
WHY IT MATTERS 
One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here. 
Industrial gases are a deceptively attractive business. The product sounds boring. The economics can be anything but. 
Customers need reliable supply. Contracts are often long term. In many industrial settings, gases are mission-critical but small compared with the cost of shutting a plant. That gives the best players steady revenue, pricing power and attractive returns on capital. 
That is why the margin gap matters so much. If two companies sell broadly similar mission-critical products into similar end markets, investors will ask why one turns more of each euro of sales into profit than the other. 
For Air Liquide, the answer may involve business mix, geography, labor productivity, project execution and historical operating choices. Elliott's presence turns those explanations into pressure points. 
There is also a broader European market angle. Activist campaigns in France are not always easy. National champions often come with political sensitivity, deep history and boards that do not enjoy being told what to do by US hedge funds. Air Liquide is also widely held by retail shareholders, which can make a traditional activist fight harder to run. 
But Elliott does not need to win a public brawl to have influence. The mere presence of a major activist can shift the conversation. Management teams suddenly find buybacks, margin targets and cost discipline moving higher up the slide deck. 
The company's growth story gives management something real to defend. AI and semiconductor demand are increasing the need for specialty gases. Energy transition projects require hydrogen, oxygen and other industrial gases. Aerospace and advanced manufacturing supply chains are also becoming more attractive. 
That's the opportunity. The risk is that heavy investment creates growth, but not enough operating leverage. If Air Liquide keeps spending big while margins lag Linde, investors may conclude that the company is funding the right markets with the wrong level of discipline. 
Elliott's likely argument is simple: Air Liquide has strong assets, strong end markets and strong strategic positioning. Now it needs stronger execution. 
WHAT'S NEXT 
October is the key moment. Air Liquide's capital markets day will be watched for margin targets, efficiency measures, portfolio moves and any buyback plans. 
The company does not need to match Linde overnight. A nine-point margin gap is too wide for one presentation to close. But investors will want to see a credible path toward narrowing it. 
For now, Elliott has put a premium on pressure. Air Liquide has the gases, the growth markets and the scale. The question is whether it can bottle more of that into profit.

content_text:
Why CMC readiness is becoming central to biopharma licensing deals
As licensing expands, manufacturing evidence is becoming a decisive test of asset value and deal confidence.
September 1, 2026 
Share
Copy Link 
Share on X 
Share on Linkedin 
Share on Facebook 
CMC readiness is becoming a decisive factor in biopharma licensing. Credit: Shutterstock 
Biopharma licensing is becoming more operational. Buyers and partners still begin with the quality of the science, but they also need evidence that an asset can be transferred, scaled and supplied without weakening its commercial potential. For outsourced assets, the right contract development and manufacturing organisation (CDMO) can strengthen confidence in technical, regulatory and financial viability, linking CMC readiness directly to asset value.
Free On-Demand Webinar
Beyond outsourcing: turning your CDMO into a value-creation engine
This on-demand webinar examines how biopharma companies can use a global CDMO to strengthen asset value and improve licensing outcomes. Join industry experts as they discuss licensing trends, CMC due diligence, manufacturing and analytical readiness, scale-up and commercialisation risks, and financing options that can help emerging biotechs conserve capital while advancing critical development milestones.
Thank you. You will receive an email shortly. Please check your inbox to download the On-Demand Webinar.
By Thermo Fisher Scientific 
This is increasingly important as pharmaceutical companies look outside their own laboratories for pipeline growth, and chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMC) should be regarded as an integral part of the asset strategy.
How licensing supports biopharma growth
In an out-licensing agreement, an innovator grants defined rights to another company, often in exchange for an upfront payment, development and commercial milestones and royalties. The structure can give a smaller developer access to capital, regulatory expertise, manufacturing capacity or commercial reach while sharing the cost and risk of advancing the asset.
In-licensing reverses the perspective; a company acquires rights to an external asset and assumes responsibility for some or all of its continued development and commercialisation. This can strengthen a pipeline faster than relying solely on internal discovery, although the licensee also inherits technical, regulatory, and market risks.
The agreement is only one point in a longer process, as asset valuation and partner identification are followed by data-room preparation, due diligence, negotiation and final contracts. The relationship then continues through development, regulatory submissions, manufacturing and launch. Decisions made before signing can therefore shape cost, timing and supply resilience years later.
Asia-Pacific has become central to this model, particularly as China develops into a major source of innovative assets. GlobalData’s 2026 conference analysis found that agreements in which US biopharma companies in-licensed an innovative drug from China reached almost 50% in 2025. The trend continued into 2026 at the JP Morgan Healthcare Conference, with AbbVie announcing a licensing agreement worth $5.6bn for RemeGen’s Phase II bispecific antibody RC148, while Novartis signed a collaboration worth more than $1.6bn with SciNeuro Pharmaceuticals for Alzheimer’s disease candidates.
The attraction also extends beyond lower development costs. GlobalData’s analysis points to faster clinical trials, stronger research capabilities and a deeper pipeline of differentiated therapies. In 2025, out-licensing activity included GSK’s $12.5bn agreement with Jiangsu Hengrui.
These cross-border deals also make CMC due diligence more important. A potential licensee must establish whether the clinical product can be reproduced at the required scale, whether data can support filings in target markets and whether manufacturing knowledge can be transferred across companies, facilities and regions. A CDMO that knows the asset can help prospective partners test those assumptions against the underlying process, capacity and regulatory evidence.
The importance of CMC due diligence and CDMOs
Financial models commonly consider revenue forecasts, development expenditure, patent life, competitive positioning and the probability of regulatory and commercial success. Weak manufacturing assumptions can affect every one of these inputs. Conversely, evidence on process robustness, cost of goods, capacity, technology transfer and regulatory readiness can strengthen confidence in the assumptions underpinning valuation.
CMC due diligence examines whether the process is understood and scalable, whether analytical methods are suitable, whether stability data supports the proposed shelf life and whether drug-substance and drug-product specifications are justified. It should also investigate impurities, degradation products, quality systems, batch history and previous regulatory interactions. These questions can reveal liabilities that are not apparent in clinical data. More importantly, that evidence is a strategic input into the asset’s technical, regulatory, and financial viability, not just a way to identify manufacturing risk.
An immature process may require additional development before pivotal trials, and incomplete stability work can restrict supply planning. Additionally, weak analytical methods can make it difficult to demonstrate comparability after a manufacturing change, and an unrealistic cost-of-goods assumption can weaken the commercial case for an otherwise promising therapy.
A recent Thermo Fisher Scientific webinar explored this in detail, recommending an audit-ready CMC package with traceable, consistent data; evidence of process robustness; early scale-up planning; and a clear narrative explaining what is known, what remains uncertain, and how gaps will be closed. That approach can help a prospective partner distinguish manageable development work from risks that could delay a programme or require a valuation adjustment. It can also strengthen confidence in scalability, cost and capacity assumptions, technology-transfer readiness and the path to commercialisation.
Anil Kane, global head of technical and scientific affairs, Pharma Services at Thermo Fisher Scientific, described CMC due diligence as a direct part of asset valuation: “The CMC package and due diligence act as a strategic gate to evaluate a variety of factors and the value of the asset.”
A CDMO with experience across development, technology transfer, regulatory filing and commercial supply can add value across the transaction. Before a deal, it can help build a licensing-ready CMC package, identify gaps and strengthen process and scale-up readiness; during diligence, it can support technical assessments, audits, gap analysis, manufacturing feasibility, cost and capacity assumptions and regulatory considerations; after signing, it can turn findings into remediation, technology transfer, scale-up, regulatory support and commercial supply.
In the webinar, Thermo Fisher Scientific gives examples of supported drug-product development, technology transfer, clinical manufacturing and scale-up for an Asian biotech’s low-dose oncology tablet. The CDMO was later audited, and its work underwent gap analysis during diligence by several prospective partners. According to the webinar, a global biopharma company ultimately acquired the asset in a deal worth more than $1bn, showing how CMC execution can drive transaction confidence and asset value.
Strategies for maximising deal success
Licensing teams can improve their position by strengthening CMC readiness before formal due diligence begins, rather than treating it only as a risk exercise. This starts with an audit-ready CMC package that brings together process knowledge, analytical methods, specifications, stability data, and batch history in a consistent, traceable form. 
The package should distinguish between resolved issues and remaining development work. It should also explain how critical quality attributes are controlled, what evidence supports process robustness and how the asset could be transferred to a new facility or manufacturing partner. Presenting these points early helps potential licensees assess the scale of the remaining work without assuming that every gap represents a fundamental weakness.
Teams also need to account for equipment differences, material sourcing, comparability requirements, available capacity and the time required to complete technical work. Responsibilities should be assigned before negotiations progress, including which activities must be completed before signing and which can continue under the new partnership.
An experienced CDMO can strengthen this preparation by testing assumptions around cost, timelines, process performance and supply. This independent challenge can expose weaknesses before they become negotiating issues and provide both parties with a more credible basis for valuation and risk allocation. After signing, the same partner can help turn diligence findings into remediation, technology transfer and scale-up, connecting assessment with execution.
Kane summarises the preparation required: “Build a licensing-ready data package, including well-organised, audit-ready documentation.” He also urged companies to prioritise transparency, so development, manufacturing and analytical information is traceable, accessible and presented consistently.
Clinical performance will remain the principal driver of an asset’s prospects. However, a well-supported route from development to commercial supply can reduce uncertainty, improve confidence in execution and make it easier for both sides to reach terms that reflect the asset’s true potential.CMC readiness and CDMO expertise can thus enhance asset value and mitigate risk.

Energy Fuels & ASM: Acquisition Adds Operating Rare Earth Metal & Alloy Capacity
September 1, 2026
Imogen Minall
Share:
Energy Fuels closes ASM acquisition, adding 1,300 tonnes per year of alloy capacity as Korean Metals Plant expansion targets 3,600 tonnes per year by the end of 2026.
Example H2
Example H3
Example H4
Energy Fuels completed its acquisition of Australian Strategic Materials (ASM), adding the operating Korean Metals Plant and the development-stage Dubbo project to its rare earth portfolio. 
The Korean Metals Plant adds 1,300 tonnes per year of existing neodymium-iron-boron alloy capacity and is being expanded toward 3,600 tonnes per year. 
Energy Fuels is targeting commissioning of the 3,600-tonne-per-year Korean Metals Plant expansion as early as the end of 2026, while approximately 5,600 tonnes per year remains a longer-term Phase III target. 
The acquisition adds commercial neodymium-praseodymium metallization and developing dysprosium and terbium metallization capabilities between Energy Fuels' oxide production and planned permanent magnet manufacturing. 
With ASM acquired, execution shifts toward expanding Korean Metals Plant capacity, advancing planned US metallization and alloy capacity, and completing the proposed Vacuumschmelze (VAC) acquisition. 
ASM Closing Converts Planned Integration Into Operating Capacity
Energy Fuels Inc. (NYSE American: UUUU | TSX: EFR | ASX: EF2) completed its acquisition of Australian Strategic Materials Limited (ASM), thereby converting part of its planned rare-earth vertical integration into owned and operated metal and alloy production. The transaction adds the Korean Metals Plant in Ochang, South Korea, with 1,300 tonnes per year of existing neodymium-iron-boron alloy capacity, alongside commercial neodymium-praseodymium metallization and developing dysprosium and terbium metallization capabilities.
The acquisition gives Energy Fuels an operating midstream step between rare earth oxide production and permanent magnet manufacturing. Korean Metals Plant metallization and alloying directly complement neodymium-praseodymium, terbium, and dysprosium oxide production and expansion initiatives at the White Mesa Mill in Utah, while permanent magnet manufacturing remains dependent on the proposed Vacuumschmelze (VAC) acquisition.
Korean Metals Plant Expansion Targets 3,600 Tonnes Per Year
The Korean Metals Plant provides Energy Fuels with existing production infrastructure rather than another development-stage asset, with the company identifying 4 furnaces, 1 strip caster, and approximately 1,300 tonnes per year of installed capacity for neodymium-iron-boron alloy. 
Energy Fuels is targeting an expansion of the Korean Metals Plant capacity to 3,600 tonnes per year, with commissioning as early as the end of 2026. Energy Fuels states that the expanded capacity could potentially produce enough neodymium-iron-boron alloy for more than 1 million electric vehicles per year, linking the expansion target to a company-stated measure of potential end-market scale.
Beyond the current expansion, the company identifies approximately 5,600 tonnes per year as a longer-term Phase III target. The capacity stages therefore remain distinct: 1,300 tonnes per year is existing capacity, 3,600 tonnes per year is the current expansion target, and approximately 5,600 tonnes per year remains a Phase III target rather than operating capacity.
Source: Energy Fuels, “Energy Fuels Completes Acquisition of Australian Strategic Materials,” August 28, 2026; Energy Fuels ASM Acquisition Presentation, January 2026. Dubbo Adds a Development-Stage Rare Earth Asset
The ASM acquisition also adds the Dubbo project in New South Wales, giving Energy Fuels a development-stage rare earth asset alongside Korean Metals Plant's operating metal and alloy capacity. Dubbo is construction-ready, with all major permits in place and a 42-year mine life.
The company reports life-of-mine (LOM) production of approximately 1,000 tonnes per year of neodymium-praseodymium, approximately 49 tonnes per year of dysprosium, and approximately 11 tonnes per year of terbium. These figures represent potential production at the development stage rather than current output, preserving the distinction between Dubbo and the Korean Metals Plant's operating capacity.
Acquisition Fills the Midstream Gap in the Mine-to-Magnet Chain
Energy Fuels' White Mesa Mill has 10,000 tonnes per year of monazite processing capacity and 1,000 tonnes per year of neodymium-praseodymium production capacity, providing existing processing and oxide-production capacity upstream of the metallization and alloying capabilities acquired through Australian Strategic Materials. The acquisition therefore connects 2 operating stages of Energy Fuels' planned rare earth chain rather than adding another exclusively development-stage capability.
The Korean Metals Plant converts this oxide-focused position into commercial metallization and alloy production, extending Energy Fuels' mine-to-magnet strategy further downstream prior to permanent magnet manufacturing. Energy Fuels is also targeting replication of Korean Metals Plant capabilities through a new American Metals Plant as market conditions warrant, which would extend its metallization and alloying footprint into the United States.
The ASM closing consequently changes the company's immediate execution test: Energy Fuels already owns commercial metal and alloy capacity, while additional Korean Metals Plant capacity, an American Metals Plant, and permanent magnet manufacturing remain dependent on future expansion, development, or transaction completion.
Source: Energy Fuels, “Energy Fuels Completes Acquisition of Australian Strategic Materials,” August 28, 2026. Permanent Magnets Remain the Final Downstream Step
Permanent magnet manufacturing remains the missing downstream stage in Energy Fuels' planned rare earth supply chain, making the proposed VAC acquisition the transaction intended to add that capability. The company continues to describe VAC as a planned acquisition and states that completion would extend Energy Fuels through the final stage of the rare earth supply chain.
The distinction defines what the ASM acquisition has and has not accomplished. Energy Fuels now owns commercial metallization and neodymium-iron-boron alloy capacity through the Korean Metals Plant, while permanent magnet manufacturing remains dependent on completion of the proposed VAC transaction.
What Comes Next
The nearest disclosed operating milestone is expansion of the Korean Metals Plant toward 3,600 tonnes per year of neodymium-iron-boron alloy capacity, with Energy Fuels targeting commissioning as early as the end of 2026. Approximately 5,600 tonnes per year remains a longer-term Phase III target, while the planned American Metals Plant is intended to replicate Korean Metals Plant capabilities in the United States as market conditions warrant.
With the ASM acquisition completed, the execution focus shifts from acquiring midstream capacity to expanding and integrating the capacity Energy Fuels now owns. The 3,600-tonne-per-year Korean Metals Plant expansion still requires commissioning; approximately 5,600 tonnes per year remains a longer-term target, and permanent magnet manufacturing remains dependent on completion of the proposed VAC acquisition.

+ 
The Korean Metals Plant has an existing neodymium-iron-boron alloy production capacity of 1,300 tonnes per year.

What does the Dubbo project add to Energy Fuels? 
+ 
Dubbo adds a development-stage Australian rare earth project that the company describes as construction-ready, with all major permits in place, a 42-year mine life, and a pre-feasibility study underway.

+ 
No. Permanent magnet manufacturing remains dependent on the proposed VAC acquisition.

LONDON | BENGALURU, India – Sept. 1, 2026 : Wipro Limited (NYSE: WIT, BSE: 507685, NSE: WIPRO), a leading AI-powered technology services and consulting company, has renewed its long-standing Digital Workplace Services contract with ABB, a global technology leader in electrification and automation. Building on an established relationship spanning multiple years, Wipro will continue delivering end-to-end AI-enabled Digital Workplace Services for ABB's global operations while further enhancing employee experience through advanced automation, AI-powered service capabilities, and workplace modernization initiatives. 
Powered by Wipro Intelligence™ , the unified suite of AI platforms, solutions and transformative offerings, this engagement will modernize ABB’s digital workplace with AI-led, experience-centric capabilities delivered through Wipro’s AI Live Workspace™ and Digital Workplace Services offerings and operationalized through WINGS, Wipro’s AI-powered delivery platform for operations. Through SmartOps, Wipro’s AIOps capability, the focus will be on more autonomous and predictive workplace services, including GenAI-powered self-service, virtual agents, auto-remediation and AI-assisted dispatch. By harnessing telemetry and usage insights, Wipro will optimize device lifecycle management and strengthen endpoint security operations, while supporting ABB’s digital transformation and sustainability ambitions. 
“As ABB operates at global scale with a highly diverse workforce, the reliability, security, and user experience of our digital workplace are critical,” said Ana Jauregui, Head of Consumer Experience, ABB. “Wipro’s ability to deliver standardized services while remaining responsive to local needs will help us drive higher productivity, improve employee satisfaction, and support our long term digital and sustainability ambitions.” 
Madhavan R, Managing Director & Country Head of Switzerland, Wipro Limited , said, “ABB and Wipro share a relationship that has grown over many years, anchored in trust, collaboration, and a common ambition to drive meaningful business outcomes. ABB’s continued confidence in Wipro reflects the strength of this enduring partnership and our shared commitment to innovation. As AI becomes a defining force in the future of work, we are bringing together our expertise and AI-led Digital Workplace capabilities to help ABB create a more intelligent, automated, resilient, and employee-centric workplace experience for colleagues across the globe.” 
This expanded engagement further reinforces Wipro's long-standing presence in the industrial and manufacturing sector, where enterprises are increasingly modernizing workplace operations to improve agility, productivity, and employee experience at a global scale.

News Releases
Sumitomo Chemical and Gutenberg Co., Ltd. Develop LCP Filament for 3D Printers
Accelerating the Development of High Value-Added Applications in Semiconductors, Communications, Next-Generation Mobility, and Other Fields 
Sep. 1, 2026
Sumitomo Chemical and Gutenberg Co., Ltd. (“Gutenberg”), which is leading the development of high-speed 3D printers produced in Japan, have jointly developed a liquid crystal polymer (LCP) filament and molding technology for 3D printers that use the FFF method (*1) . The Company will accelerate the development of applications in next-generation fields, including functional components that contribute to advances in semiconductors and physical AI.
3D-printed parts 
Robot hand housing 
In recent years, materials capable of handling complex geometries, achieving weight reductions, and integrating parts have been receiving increased interest across advanced industrial fields. For this reason, design and manufacturing using 3D printers have attracted increasing attention. Amid this trend, there is a demand for not only freedom of design, but also for high functionality in resin materials themselves. LCP is a super engineering plastic that combines heat resistance, high strength, low dielectric constant and low dissipation factor, and excellent dimensional stability. As a material for 3D printers, however, its use has been limited due to difficulties in filament formation and molding.
To address these challenges, Sumitomo Chemical has developed a material design and filament formation technology for LCP suited to additive manufacturing. The Company also collaborated with Gutenberg, which develops, manufactures, and sells industrial 3D printers, to examine the molding process and establish a technology that enables stable molding while controlling the unique molecular orientation of LCP. This technology achieves high thermal conductivity and strength comparable to that of aluminum alloys (*2) , while also maintaining lightweight properties. This makes it possible to create complex shapes that are difficult to achieve with injection molding, while also meeting the needs of low-volume, high-mix production.
Going forward, Sumitomo Chemical will expand its efforts into a wide range of fields, including peripheral components for semiconductor manufacturing, humanoid robot-related components that are expected to be put into practical use as physical AI advances, the communications field, and next-generation mobility fields such as eVTOL (*3) . In addition, the Company will accelerate the development of new applications by advancing evaluations of its filament and molded products in collaboration with customers. The Company plans to begin providing samples of this filament in 2026, and it is also looking ahead to future expansion into the space and defense fields.
Sumitomo Chemical will continue to promote the provision of innovative materials and solutions that support next-generation manufacturing. In doing so, the Company will contribute to the creation of new value and the development of society and industry.
(*1) A 3D printing method in which thermoplastic resin is melted, extruded from a nozzle, and stacked layer by layer. 
(*2) The Company evaluated the fracture strength of LCP and aluminum alloy under certain conditions using a test method compliant with standards set by the International Organization for Standardization. 
(*3) Electric Vertical Take-Off and Landing aircraft, commonly referred to as flying cars.

Novartis pauses autoimmune cell therapy studies after deaths 
Uncertainty surrounds timeline of fatalities as firms withhold further comment
September 01, 2026 at 8:00 am 
Share current article via Email Share current article via Facebook Share current article via Twitter Share current article via LinkedIn 
Reuters
News Agency
Enter fullscreen mode displaying this image. Expand 
The Swiss pharmaceutical company temporarily halted the studies after learning of three fatal cases of a severe immune response. Picture: 
Novartis paused eight clinical trials of an experimental therapy targeting autoimmune and neurological disorders in late August after three patients died, the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported on Tuesday.
The Swiss pharmaceutical company temporarily halted the studies after learning of three fatal cases of a severe immune response, the report said, citing a spokesperson. It wasn’t immediately clear when the deaths occurred.
The experimental treatment is called chimeric antigen receptor T-cell, or CAR-T.
CAR-T therapies modify a patient’s immune cells to recognise a specific target and destroy cancer cells.
Novartis is conducting “a comprehensive review of the observed safety events”, the spokesperson told WSJ, describing the fatal immune response as a known safety risk in CAR-T therapies.
According to the report, the company said it is working with independent safety boards overseeing each paused study and sharing what it knows with regulators.
Bristol-Myers Squibb (BMY) also paused similar trials of its CAR-T treatment in autoimmune disorders as a precautionary measure, the newspaper said.
Novartis and BMY did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

title: Applied Materials Touts 3D Scaling Technologies, Develops New Materials for HBM and CPO - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

query: "Applied Materials" (Korea OR Korean) after:2026-09-01 before:2026-10-01
content_text:
Mukund Srinivasan, global group vice president of Packaging and Integrated Materials Solutions at Applied Materials. (Photo: THE ELEC) 
Applied Materials has completed preparations for four key technologies needed for next-generation three-dimensional (3D) semiconductor scaling. The company is also accelerating workforce and infrastructure expansion in line with recent capacity increases by its Korean customers.
Mukund Srinivasan, global group vice president of Packaging and Integrated Materials Solutions at Applied Materials, said at a media briefing at Oakwood Premier Coex Center on Aug. 31 that artificial intelligence (AI) models are becoming increasingly compute-intensive, with their power consumption rising exponentially. "The solution to the industry's key challenge of minimizing power consumption per bit of data is 3D scaling," he said.
The proliferation of AI is exacerbating the "memory wall," a bottleneck between computing and memory. Overcoming it requires more efficient data transmission that moves information quickly while consuming less power. Applied Materials said logic chips, memory and packaging are all rapidly transitioning to 3D structures.
The company also outlined four key challenges in implementing 3D structures and the technologies it has developed to address them. "The most important innovations for 3D scaling are, first, new materials development; second, actual process innovation; then angstrom-level (Å, 0.1 nanometers) process control of processes and equipment; and optimization at each process step," Srinivasan said. "Applied has considerable confidence in its core unit processes and materials, and we are confident that we can also solve the challenges of integrating them."
◇ New Materials for HBM and CPO 
Kim Ji-hye, executive director at Applied Materials Korea, moderates the media briefing. (Photo: THE ELEC) 
New materials development is aimed at easing interconnect bottlenecks inside and outside chips. Resistance and capacitance need to be reduced to increase signal transmission speeds and lower power losses. Applied Materials is seeking solutions through advanced thin-film and plating technologies and new materials research and development (R&D).
The Producer Avila 2 plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) system is one such solution. It can deposit oxide and nitride thin films at low temperatures on the backside of high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Core dies, or DRAM chips, used in HBM are about one-25th the thickness of conventional DRAM dies, making them susceptible to warpage. Applied Materials' solutions also include the Nokota VMax 2 electrochemical deposition (ECD) system for copper plating of ultra-fine through-silicon vias (TSVs) measuring 3 micrometers or less.
More recently, the company has been jointly researching new optical waveguide materials with customers for co-packaged optics (CPO). CPO is a next-generation technology that integrates optical and high-performance electronic chips in a single package. Applied Materials is also developing highly thermally conductive insulating materials that maximize heat dissipation while maintaining electrical insulation to address HBM thermal issues.
◇ 3D Structure and Hybrid Bonding Technologies in Place 
HBM and CPO models. (Photo: THE ELEC) 
The second area, process innovation, requires technologies capable of forming complex 3D structures. Applied Materials has developed and commercialized selective processes that can treat specific areas within 3D structures, as well as bonding technologies that reduce the spacing between chips to near zero.
In particular, the Centura Prime Epi selective epitaxy system for DRAM peripheral circuitry selectively grows silicon germanium (SiGe) and phosphorus-doped silicon (Si:P) in transistor electrode regions, or sources and drains. The technology enables next-generation semiconductor manufacturing by introducing impurities into silicon and precisely controlling their concentration to tune the electrical properties of semiconductors.
Applied Materials also offers Kinex, an integrated die-to-wafer (D2W) hybrid bonding cluster system. D2W bonding directly joins copper and dielectric materials between chips, maximizing input/output (I/O) density and reducing signal delays compared with microbumps. Kinex integrates plasma activation, cleaning, D2W bonding and metrology into a single system, cutting queue time from 13 hours to one hour.
"Applied has a complete portfolio of products for both D2W and wafer-to-wafer (W2W)," Srinivasan said. "We are helping customers more easily determine which combinations and approaches they want to adopt."
Third, as logic and memory processes become more advanced, equipment capable of real-time control and measurement of errors at the nanometer and angstrom scales has become essential. Applied Materials has prepared the Opta Quad chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) system, the VeritySEM 7AP e-beam critical-dimension metrology system and the SEMVision G7AP e-beam defect analysis system. Opta Quad CMP can be used for hybrid bonding and TSVs, VeritySEM 7AP for HBM and chiplet substrates, and SEMVision G7AP for silicon, organic and glass substrates.
◇ EPIC Center and ACCK Link Up as Korea Hiring Continues 
Park Kwang-sun, president of Applied Materials Korea. (Photo: THE ELEC) 
The final area, optimization at each process step, involves integrating interactions among semiconductor manufacturing processes beyond the individual equipment level. Applied Materials is preparing for this through its EPIC (Equipment and Process Innovation and Commercialization) Center and Applied Collaboration Center Korea (ACCK).
Applied Materials' EPIC Center is a $5 billion R&D facility. Companies including Samsung Electronics, SK hynix and Micron are participating. The facility is under construction and is scheduled to open in Silicon Valley in October. It will allow semiconductor companies to jointly coordinate the entire process from early-stage materials development to device design, deposition, planarization and bonding, and validate technologies for mass production. The goal is to significantly shorten the time needed to commercialize new technologies.
ACCK is a next-generation semiconductor R&D collaboration hub being established in Osan, Gyeonggi Province. It will receive foundational technologies and innovative materials developed at the EPIC Center in Silicon Valley and jointly develop them with Korean customers through technology validation. "Once ACCK in Korea is completed, we will connect foundational research and materials innovations developed at the EPIC Center with Korean customers through ACCK in Osan," said Park Kwang-sun, president of Applied Materials Korea. "We will strengthen the support system so new technologies can be directly linked to our customers' mass-production lines in Korea and maximize the pace of innovation."
"We are also making various efforts to ensure there are no gaps in workforce and technical support as our customers expand globally," Park added. "We are having in-depth discussions about workforce expansion not only internally but also with universities and customers, so we do not expect major difficulties."

Merck Korea Launches Campaign to Mark World Multiple Sclerosis Day 
by Koo Kyo Yun 
Updated 2026/06/01 11:23 
Merck Korea Healthcare held an event commemorating the 18th World Multiple Sclerosis Day on May 30. / Photo = Merck Korea Healthcare 
Merck Korea Healthcare said on the 1st that it conducted the Overcoming Multiple Sclerosis campaign throughout May in collaboration with the Korean Multiple Sclerosis Association and the Korean Society for Neuroimmunology to mark World Multiple Sclerosis Day on May 30.
The campaign was organized to promote a proper understanding of multiple sclerosis and raise awareness of the importance of early diagnosis and long-term disease management. Merck Korea has continued activities to raise disease awareness since 2018, and this year, the three organizations joined forces to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Korean Multiple Sclerosis Association's founding.
Major programs included the distribution of educational content through the Korean Society for Neuroimmunology's official YouTube channel, as well as an event commemorating the 18th World Multiple Sclerosis Day held at the Korea Arts Center for Persons with Disabilities. The event, which focused on diagnosis, featured lectures by Professor Kim Ki-hoon of Yonsei University College of Medicine's Sinchon Severance Hospital, public relations director of the Korean Society for Neuroimmunology, and Professor Kwon Yong-jin of Seoul National University Hospital's Public Healthcare Center, along with patient story sharing and digital education. Employees of Merck Korea's Specialty business unit and the company's volunteer club, '머크ON,' participated at the event venue to support its operation.
In addition, Merck Korea conducted an internal campaign throughout May. Employees achieved the goal of walking 5 million steps over the month through a 'Walking Challenge' to cheer on patients, and participated in a quiz on early management, taking time to experience the difficulties patients face in their daily lives.
Christoph Hamann, head of Merck Korea Healthcare, said, "Based on its expertise in neuroimmunology, Merck Korea has contributed to improving the treatment environment in the country by providing innovative treatment options. We will continue to take the lead in improving treatment access for patients with rare, severe and hard-to-treat diseases and in raising disease awareness."

EUV Mask Blanks Market Report Scope & Overview: 
The EUV Mask Blanks Market size was valued at USD 232.00 Million in 2025 and is expected to reach USD 864.00 Million by 2035, growing at a CAGR of 14.05% from 2026-2035.
EUV mask blanks constitute a foundational category within advanced semiconductor lithography, serving as the ultra-flat, multilayer substrates that carry the reflective coatings ultimately patterned into photomasks used in extreme ultraviolet exposure systems. Rising adoption of EUV lithography for sub-5-nanometer logic and memory production, expanding global EUV-capable fab capacity, and the relentless demand for higher density semiconductor devices continue to broaden the industrial base requiring these precision substrates. Foundries, integrated device manufacturers, and an expanding base of research institutions rely on these blanks to achieve the defect densities and flatness tolerances essential to reliable advanced-node chip production.
⮞ In January 2024, AGC Inc. began a phased expansion of EUV lithography photomask blank production capacity at its subsidiary AGC Electronics, targeting an approximately 30% capacity increase by 2025. The company stated the investment reflects continued strong demand growth for EUV mask blanks supporting higher-performance semiconductor manufacturing.

The company continues to position itself as a leading global supplier of photomasks serving advanced logic and memory production. 
EUV Mask Blanks Market Segment Analysis
By Type, the Multilayer Mask Blanks segment dominated the market with a 68.50% share in 2025, while the Phase-Shifting Mask Blanks segment is the fastest growing with a CAGR of 15.80% during 2026-2035.
By Substrate Material, the Low Thermal Expansion Material segment dominated the market with a 72.40% share in 2025, while the Fused Silica segment is the fastest growing with a CAGR of 14.60% during 2026-2035.
By Application, the Logic/IC segment dominated the market with a 68.60% share in 2025, while the Memory Devices segment is the fastest growing with a CAGR of 15.90% during 2026-2035.
By End-User, the Foundries segment dominated the market with a 54.80% share in 2025, while the Research Institutions segment is the fastest growing with a CAGR of 10.80% during 2026-2035.
By Type, Multilayer Mask Blanks Dominates the Market and Phase-Shifting Mask Blanks Grows Fastest 
Multilayer Mask Blanks dominated the market in 2025, a position built on their role as the standard substrate configuration comprising 40 to 50 alternating layers of silicon and molybdenum required to achieve the reflective properties essential to EUV exposure. Foundries favour this blank type precisely because it delivers the proven optical performance required across virtually every current-generation EUV lithography application, a combination that continues to make multilayer blanks the default specification across leading-edge logic and memory production worldwide, even as phase-shifting variants continue to expand around it for specialized applications.
Phase-Shifting Mask Blanks are projected to be the fastest-growing type category over the forecast period. Rising demand for improved pattern contrast and resolution enhancement continues to expand the addressable application base for this blank type as chipmakers push toward increasingly fine feature geometries at sub-3-nanometer nodes. As foundries increasingly require finer pattern fidelity to support next-generation logic and memory architectures, phase-shifting blanks continue closing the gap with conventional multilayer blanks in overall market demand.
By Substrate Material, Low Thermal Expansion Material Dominates the Market and Fused Silica Grows Fastest 
Low Thermal Expansion Material dominated the market in 2025. This substrate category remains the technically essential foundation for EUV mask blanks, as the ultra-low thermal expansion glass plate must maintain dimensional stability throughout repeated exposure to intense EUV radiation without introducing pattern placement errors. This fundamental technical requirement continues to sustain low thermal expansion material as the dominant substrate category across virtually every EUV mask blank application worldwide.
Fused Silica substrates are expected to be the fastest-growing substrate material category over the forecast period. Continued advancement in synthetic quartz manufacturing processes continues to improve flatness and reduce defect density relative to conventional substrate alternatives, expanding the addressable application base for this material category. As manufacturers continue refining fused silica production techniques to meet increasingly stringent quality requirements, this segment continues to close the gap with low thermal expansion material in overall market demand.
By Application, Logic/IC Dominates the Market and Memory Devices Grows Fastest 
Logic/IC applications dominated the market in 2025. The relentless push toward smaller semiconductor process nodes below 5 nanometers continues to represent the single largest driver of overall EUV mask blank consumption worldwide, as leading-edge logic foundries require increasingly sophisticated photomask capability to support advanced chip architectures. This foundational role continues to sustain logic and integrated circuit applications as the largest application category by a clear margin across the broader market.
Memory Devices applications are projected to expand fastest over the forecast period. Rising adoption of EUV lithography across advanced DRAM and NAND flash production continues to expand the addressable application base for this category as memory manufacturers increasingly adopt EUV patterning to achieve the density improvements required for next-generation memory architectures. As memory manufacturers continue extending EUV adoption beyond its historical logic-focused origins, this segment continues to close the gap with logic and IC applications in overall market demand.
By End-User, Foundries Dominates the Market and Research Institutions Grows Fastest 
Foundries dominated the market in 2025. The scale of leading-edge chip production concentrated among a small number of pure-play foundries continues to represent the single largest source of EUV mask blank demand worldwide, given these companies' central role in manufacturing advanced logic chips for a broad customer base of fabless semiconductor design companies. This concentrated demand structure continues to sustain foundries as the clear leading end-user category across the broader market.
Research Institutions are expected to be the fastest-growing end-user category over the forecast period. Rising government semiconductor competitiveness initiatives across Europe, Japan, and the United States continue to expand EUV research program activity as governments increasingly fund domestic semiconductor research capability. As academic research institutions, government labs, and EUV mask blank evaluation programs continue proliferating globally, this end-user category continues to expand its share of overall market demand.

North America EUV Mask Blanks Market Insights 
North America represents a significant regional market for EUV mask blanks, anchored by the United States' concentration of leading semiconductor equipment innovators and growing domestic advanced photomask manufacturing capability. The United States accounts for the substantial majority of regional demand, reflecting both its semiconductor equipment leadership and its role hosting growing domestic fabrication capacity under federal semiconductor competitiveness initiatives.
Canada and Mexico contribute limited additional regional volume through participation in broader North American semiconductor supply chain activity. Continued domestic investment in advanced photomask manufacturing capability is expected to support steady regional market development even as growth in percentage terms trails faster-scaling Asia Pacific markets building out fabrication capacity from a considerably larger existing base.
Europe EUV Mask Blanks Market Insights 
Europe holds a meaningful share of the global market, underpinned by growing government semiconductor research funding and continued advancement in EUV mask blank evaluation programs supported by domestic research institutions. Germany's substantial semiconductor equipment and materials research base anchors regional demand, supported by government initiatives aimed at strengthening European semiconductor supply chain resilience.
Other major European markets contribute additional demand as regional semiconductor competitiveness initiatives continue expanding research institution participation in EUV mask blank evaluation and qualification programs. Continued European Union investment in domestic semiconductor research capability supports steady regional demand for EUV mask blank evaluation and testing activity.
MEA & Latin America EUV Mask Blanks Market Insights 
The Middle East & Africa market remains limited in scale, with activity concentrated in Israel, where established semiconductor research and development operations continue to support modest regional demand for EUV mask blank evaluation and testing activity.
Latin America's market remains the smallest globally, reflecting the region's limited concentration of advanced semiconductor fabrication capacity. Gradual growth in regional semiconductor research interest continues to support minimal but steady regional market development over the forecast period.
Market Dynamics 
Growth Drivers: Advanced Node Adoption and EUV Fab Capacity Expansion 
The growing need for increased density and higher power of semiconductor products forms the first driving force behind market development, since the number of manufacturing facilities equipped with EUV is steadily increasing from about 35 in 2025 to around 75-85 by 2034. At the same time, the semiconductor industry continues working toward developing sub-5-nanometer and even sub-3-nanometer nodes, which can be achieved only through using EUV and its associated masks supply chain.
Increasing activities within governmental semiconductor competitiveness programs in Europe, Japan, and the US form another major factor that stimulates demand. At the moment, the governments still continue funding their research institutions' work on evaluation of EUV mask blanks. Increasing use of EUV technology in memory device manufacturing helps market grow.
Restraints: Capacity Constraints and Defect Density Challenges 
Capacity constraints remain a genuine restraint on market growth, as qualified blank production lines couple to scanner and foundry roadmaps over five-to-seven-year cycles, meaning capacity cannot be summoned quickly to meet sudden demand spikes. This dynamic is compounded by the concentrated oligopoly structure of the supply chain, where a small number of vertically integrated suppliers control the substantial majority of global coated-blank production capacity.
Defect density challenges present a further restraint, as defect densities beyond acceptable thresholds can force fabs to scrap a meaningful share of EUV mask blanks, inflating costs and delaying tape-out schedules. This requires suppliers to sustain substantial ongoing investment in defectivity reduction technology, spanning cleaning process optimization and inspection capability that can meaningfully affect production yield and cost structures.
Opportunities: High-NA EUV Technology and Supply Chain Diversification 
Continued advancement of high-NA EUV compatible mask blanks offers a substantial opportunity, as suppliers developing blanks meeting the demanding specifications of next-generation high-numerical-aperture scanner systems stand to capture meaningful new demand from foundries pursuing the most advanced available lithography capability. Suppliers increasingly view this technology not as a novelty feature but as a genuine strategic necessity for maintaining relevance in next-generation semiconductor manufacturing.
The rising importance of supply chain diversification presents a further avenue for growth, as governments and foundries alike increasingly seek to reduce concentration risk associated with the current oligopoly supply structure. This diversification pathway continues to open opportunities for new entrants and research institutions pursuing alternative substrate and coating technologies, even as established suppliers continue to dominate near-term commercial supply.
